items.title: David Jones goes into administration, with store closures expected and thousands of jobs at risk
items.summary: Future of Australia’s upmarket department store in jeopardy after years of steep losses, and outer suburban and regional locations vulnerable Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Australia’s premier upmarket department store David Jones has collapsed into voluntary administration, putting thousands of jobs at risk amid warnings “difficult decisions” lie ahead to salvage the 188-year-old retailer. The upheaval follows years of steep losses and underperforming stores that left the heritage retailer falling behind on rent, culminating in a breakdown of negotiations with its primary landlord, Westfield owner Scentre Group. Continue reading...
items.body:
Australia’s premier upmarket department store David Jones has collapsed into voluntary administration, putting thousands of jobs at risk amid warnings “difficult decisions” lie ahead to salvage the 188-year-old retailer.
The upheaval follows years of steep losses and underperforming stores that left the heritage retailer falling behind on rent, culminating in a breakdown of negotiations with its primary landlord, Westfield owner Scentre Group.
Staff were informed on Thursday that the David Jones board had appointed administrators from McGrathNicol, before the retailer’s main financier promptly installed FTI Consulting as receivers.
Under the dual appointment, FTI will take day-to-day control of operations, while administrators McGrathNicol seek a buyer or fresh injection of capital.
Christopher Hill, of FTI Consulting, said the process allowed for “an opportunity to restructure the business”.
“We will manage this process carefully, mindful of the impact on some stakeholders but also recognising the need for difficult decisions,” Hill said.
The process will almost certainly trigger immediate store closures, though receivers will try keep the core network open.
Analysts expect closures to hit outer suburban and regional mall locations hardest, likely sparing premier CBD flagship stores.
David Jones employs more than 6,000 staff across a network of 38 stores.
The David Jones chief executive, Erica Berchtold, said there was a “well developed plan on how to reset the business” and that the retailer would work with the administrators, receivers and its secured lender.
Creditors are scheduled to meet next week, according to the Shop, Distributive and Allied Employees’ Association.
The national secretary of the SDA, Gerard Dwyer, told the ABC the top priority was to retain as many jobs as possible.
“We do not want to see the end of David Jones, so perhaps it is a smaller model that then rebuilds and goes from there,” Dwyer said.
“Smaller is better than no David Jones, and a smaller David Jones can then deal with some of the challenges that they’ve obviously been facing.”
The administration could leave unsecured creditors with substantial losses, with unpaid product suppliers, some of which had already begun redirecting stock to their own retail outlets, and shoppers holding unredeemed gift vouchers most at risk.
Gift cards may be ‘worthless’ soon
Angus Kidman, from consumer comparison site Finder, said customers with David Jones gift cards should use them as soon as possible.
“If the business doesn’t find a buyer, that gift card will almost certainly be worthless,” Kidman said.
“Stores appear to be accepting gift cards for now, so don’t delay. That also applies to any discounts you’ve earned through David Jones Rewards.”
The collapse marks the first time David Jones has been in administration, having previously weathered nearly two centuries while cycling through almost every type of ownership model, from public listing to foreign conglomerate ownership and, most recently, private equity.
Anchorage Capital Partners, which bought David Jones from South Africa’s Woolworths in 2023, has now lost operational control after failing to turn the struggling retailer around.
It could re-bid for the business through the administration process or a rival buyer, such as billionaire businessman Solomon Lew, who controls Myer, may get involved.
The retailer’s main landlord, Scentre, said on Wednesday that David Jones had not paid rent since September.
“We have made a generous offer to Anchorage Capital that would have facilitated the continuation of David Jones trading and that offer has disappointingly been rejected by them,” Scentre said in a statement.

items.title: OECD: AI compute now a strategic asset as UK bets £2bn
items.summary: <p>Artificial intelligence (AI) compute has become a strategic national asset, with venture capital for AI infrastructure more than doubling year-on-year to $123.9bn in 2025. Meanwhile, the UK’s commitment to spend up to £2bn on its Compute Roadmap is one of the leading bets placed by governments around the world.</p> <p>That’s according to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), which published its <em>Digital economy and society outlook 2026</em> today.</p> <p>In the report, the OECD says AI compute now sits alongside data, algorithms and skills as a determinant of who can build and deploy advanced AI systems. It says venture capital investment in AI firms in IT infrastructure and hosting rose from $54.5bn in 2024 to $123.9bn in 2025, which is the largest increase since 2012.</p> <p>The report namechecks the <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/uk-compute-roadmap/uk-compute-roadmap">
items.body:
Victoria - Fotolia
OECD: AI compute now a strategic asset as UK bets £2bn
Venture capital for artificial intelligence firms in IT infrastructure and hosting rose from $54.5bn to $123.9bn, while the OECD says compute now shapes which countries can build advanced AI
Artificial intelligence (AI) compute has become a strategic national asset, with venture capital for AI infrastructure more than doubling year-on-year to $123.9bn in 2025. Meanwhile, the UK’s commitment to spend up to £2bn on its Compute Roadmap is one of the leading bets placed by governments around the world.
That’s according to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), which published its Digital economy and society outlook 2026 today.
In the report, the OECD says AI compute now sits alongside data, algorithms and skills as a determinant of who can build and deploy advanced AI systems. It says venture capital investment in AI firms in IT infrastructure and hosting rose from $54.5bn in 2024 to $123.9bn in 2025, which is the largest increase since 2012.
The report namechecks the UK Compute Roadmap, launched in 2025 with up to £2bn pledged to “deliver a holistic and user-centred compute ecosystem” and £1bn to expand the AI Research Resource, plus a new national supercomputing service. It also notes the emergence of neocloud providers of infrastructure purpose-built for AI workloads, such as the UK’s Nscale, the US’s CoreWeave and Netherlands-headquartered Nebius.
The OECD is an intergovernmental body whose member governments use it to agree non-binding standards for digital policy. Its reports do not set law, but governments fold their recommendations into regulation – such as the EU AI Act – so the organisation is an early indicator of auditability and data governance requirements that can later become compliance obligations.
The OECD warns in the report that sizeable capital investment in infrastructure, networking and energy access gives traditional hyperscalers a considerable market advantage, which is compounded by developer ecosystems and hardware partnerships that build dependencies. Newer AI-specific providers may expand, it says, but buyers will likely continue to rely on existing hyperscaler capacity – a familiar dynamic for UK organisations balancing cloud lock-in against AI ambition.
The report flags two bottlenecks that may limit compute performance. The first is that accelerator performance has tripled every two years while memory (DRAM) has scaled at just 1.6 times over the same period – a gap it calls “the memory wall”, which can leave processors idle and waiting for data. Moving data between chips forms a second constraint – “the interconnect wall”, which slows distributed training and inference across racks and nodes.
For IT leaders, it says, compute also collides with energy and planning. The OECD notes that hyperscale datacentre buildouts can take up to three years, while securing multi-gigawatt power can take more than four – a mismatch that already shapes grid connection queues and the UK’s push towards 6GW of AI-capable capacity.
“Alongside data, algorithms and skills, AI compute has emerged as a strategic asset with profound implications for innovation and competitiveness,” the report says.
Other government investments in AI include Canada, which committed C$2bn (approx. £1bn) to a Sovereign AI Compute Strategy in 2024; the EU, which will channel €7bn (approx. £5.5bn) through its EuroHPC joint undertaking for 2021-27; and the US, which backs the Stargate datacentre venture.
The OECD report finds that 60% of member countries now assign national digital strategy to a dedicated digital ministry, up from 24% in 2016, and that cyber security has risen to the second-highest policy priority.
The scale of the figures demands caution, the report says. “Figures often reflect announcements and commitments rather than implementation,” it says, with delivery dependent on supply chain resilience, energy and water availability, and shifting national priorities.
On that reading, the investment surge can be viewed as a statement of intent rather than evidence of built capacity. Turning the UK’s £2bn into operational infrastructure will depend on grid and planning constraints that decide whether promised datacentres arrive on time.
Read more about AI compute and datacentres
- Hit the north! UK datacentre focus shifts to M62 and points north: Barbour ABI data shows an 8GW datacentre pipeline concentrated in the north and Scotland, with London and the M4 corridor about 25% of projected capacity.
- Enormous AI growth zone datacentre gets planning approval: A planned 1GW AI growth zone facility – equal to more than 2% of current UK electricity demand – gains consent.

items.title: Australia's oldest department store David Jones folds after 188 years
items.summary: The brand's 38 physical stores and online site will continue to operate while receivers review its operations.
items.body:
Australia's oldest department store David Jones folds after 188 years
- Published
David Jones, Australia's oldest department store chain, has gone into voluntary administration, putting thousands of jobs at risk.
It comes after years of financial struggles for the 188-year-old retailer - known locally as DJs - as customers desert traditional shops for online shopping.
David Jones's physical and online stores will continue to operate while receivers FTI Consulting review the company, said voluntary administrators McGrathNicol.
"David Jones is an iconic company and so many Australians have stories and memories of visiting DJ's stores," said its CEO Erica Berthold, adding the brand has a "well-developed plan" to "reset the business for the future".
Berthold thanked "customers, our team members and our partners for their continued support of David Jones through this period".
David Jones employs about 6,000 staff and has 38 physical stores, with 17 of those in Westfield shopping centres.
Hours before the board voted to go into administration, Scentre - which owns Westfield - said the retailer had not paid its rent for October and was "therefore in breach" of its tenancy agreement.
"We understand the current retail trading environment, rising costs, a significant and outdated retail footprint, and supply chain challenges have led to this point," said Christopher Hill from receivers FTI Consulting.
By appointing administrators and receivers, David Jones will get "breathing space" and a chance to restructure the business, Hill said.
For many Australians, David Jones - and its trademark black-and-white houndstooth design - represented luxury.
But its collapse signalled the "death knell" for the department store format, said Jana Bowden, who teaches marketing at Macquarie University's Business School.
"It was once the epitome of glamour shopping in Australia - the Aussie version of Harrods," she said, "a place you would go to see and be a part of the glitz and glamour, where you could marvel at all the premium luxury labels, and feel like you'd made it."
Visiting the flagship city stores in Sydney and Melbourne was also a ritual for many Australian families, especially to see the festive Christmas window displays.
"People would travel from hours away from the city just to see those windows and experience the magic," Bowden said, but in recent years, the brand had lost its shine.
"The city stores have retained their upper end airs and graces, but the suburban stores leave a lot to be desired â they're mundane, they lack excitement and there's definitely no glitz," she said.
During Queen Elizabeth II's first visit to Sydney in 1954, the then-27-year-old monarch attended a banquet dinner on the seventh floor of the Elizabeth St store, according to the Sydney Morning Herald.

items.title: Once it was a £1 hanger. Now it’s a £15 locker. Why do cloakrooms cost so much on a night out?
items.summary: The cost of checking your coat or bag is galloping ahead of other – also rising – prices at venues. We explain the surprisingly complex reasons why Not long ago, it cost just £2 to put a coat or a heavily stuffed tote bag in a cloakroom on a night out. But over the course of the 2020s, that cost has increased to more than £13 in some UK venues. At the Outernet Live venue complex in London’s Soho, it costs £11 to put a bag in a large locker. It’s £9 at east London nightclub Fold, and at north London’s Drumsheds, the UK’s biggest nightclub, they cost up to £13.20 . At the Warehouse Project in Manchester, large bags must be stored at a nearby Premier Inn at £11.99 per locker. Manchester’s Co-op Live Arena has a dedicated bag storage facility which costs £15 for large bags. It’s £9.99 near the 3,000-capacity Edinburgh Playhouse and £9.90 at Testbed in Leeds. How have double-digit cloakroom costs like these been normalised? Continue reading...
items.body:
Not long ago, it cost just £2 to put a coat or a heavily stuffed tote bag in a cloakroom on a night out. But over the course of the 2020s, that cost has increased to more than £13 in some UK venues.
At the Outernet Live venue complex in London’s Soho, it costs £11 to put a bag in a large locker. It’s £9 at east London nightclub Fold, and at north London’s Drumsheds, the UK’s biggest nightclub, they cost up to £13.20 . At the Warehouse Project in Manchester, large bags must be stored at a nearby Premier Inn at £11.99 per locker. Manchester’s Co-op Live Arena has a dedicated bag storage facility which costs £15 for large bags. It’s £9.99 near the 3,000-capacity Edinburgh Playhouse and £9.90 at Testbed in Leeds. How have double-digit cloakroom costs like these been normalised?
The price rises are helping to push average spending per head on a night out from £20.95 in 2020 to £28.06 in 2026, according to Night Time Industries Association. “For years, nightlife businesses have faced relentless increases in the cost of operating, from energy and employment to taxation, business rates and supply chains,” says chief executive Michael Kill. “Many have had no choice but to pass some of those costs on to consumers simply to keep their doors open. But the reality is that consumers have now hit an affordability ceiling.”
With consumers spending less on alcohol, locker systems and cloakrooms offer premises a way to make some of that money back, but, Kill says, “the consumer cannot be the industry’s financial shock absorber indefinitely”.
UK storage policy changed after the 2017 attack at an Ariana Grande concert in Manchester Arena which killed 22 people and injured more than 1,000. “Martyn’s law” legislation requires “appropriate public protection measures” at public events to reduce the risk and impact of terror attacks. It led to many venues – including the nationwide network of 18 Academy Music Group sites – banning bags over A4 size entirely and offloading them to external lockers or storage partners. In London, these are often kebab shops, restaurants and barbers.
Carrie Wang, a London-based spin instructor, was buzzing to see Hot Chip at O2 Academy Brixton until she learned her near-empty tote bag had to be stored in a kebab shop round the corner. “I was fuming,” Wang says. “They charged me £10 and it wasn’t a proper facility, it was just a random storage room – it’s not like they had lockers and my things were actually safe there.” Academy Music Group did not respond to multiple requests for comment.
Ahmed Khan is the owner of Kentish Delight, a kebab shop in Kentish Town. He says that in 2022, O2 Kentish Town Forum’s management asked if he had any spare space in the takeaway. “They had a look and said my premises are perfect and secure for the customer – and I said yes, why not?” Khan charges £5 per bag and says nothing has ever gone missing. “Although the bag people never buy kebabs.”
The high costs and added logistics mean that some people are taking risks with their belongings. At an AEW wrestling event at Wembley Arena, fans were directed to a nearby Premier Inn to stow their bags, at £10 a pop with long queues.
Soul singer Danny Toeman decided to stuff his rucksack behind a carpark vending machine. “I could stuff most of the valuable contents into my pockets,” says Toeman. “So I thought: let’s just stash it somewhere and if it gets stolen, so what?”
That in itself is a security risk – if staff had seen Toeman’s backpack, the venue could have been evacuated. But it’s become commonplace. One Reddit user opted to hide their bag outside the O2 Academy in Southampton. “They will literally not let you in,” they wrote. “I was forced to leave it outside the building entirely and it was stolen when I came out.”
Willem Pelle is head of sales at eLockers, a Dutch company working with many UK nightclubs including Drumsheds, Fold and Warehouse Project. “When we expanded into the UK, we saw that many venues were facing staffing challenges following Covid, making traditional cloakrooms increasingly difficult to operate,” Pelle says.
London is their main UK market, with Manchester a close second. Pelle says there is typically no upfront cost for the venue, which gets to share the takings with eLockers, adding: “It’s important that the pricing works for both the venue and its customers, while creating a sustainable additional revenue stream.”
Some clubbers have reported benefits to lockers, such as those at Drumsheds, where you can put stuff in and out – allowing for outfit changes during an event. But not all venues opt to install expensive locker systems. At Hackney Bath House, the cloakroom is free. Sneaky Pete’s in Edinburgh installed lockers in 2012 and still charge £2 per locker. Peckham’s 200-capacity club the Carpet Shop charges £3 per item: “No need to charge more, it’s a tiny bit of space and a rail,” says general manager Cam Prentis.
He sees the cloakroom as a valuable part of the club experience in its own right. Upstairs and away from the bustle, it’s where staff and punters can have a break and a chat. “Whoever’s on the cloakroom has their own music playing,” Cam says. Unlike at an unstaffed array of lockers or the back room of a kebab shop, “it’s a vibe up there”.
Some names have been changed

items.title: Poundland could be nationalised to save it from collapse, says Labour business minister
items.summary: Poundland could be nationalised to save it from collapse, a government minister suggested today.
items.body:
Poundland could be nationalised to save it from collapse, says Labour business minister
Poundland could be nationalised to save it from collapse, a government minister suggested today.
Business minister Lord Leong refused to rule out a taxpayer subsidy or even full-blown state control of the troubled discount chain.
The comment was seized on by the Tories as evidence of Labour chaos and a lack of understanding of business.
It came as Andy Burnham said the government was ‘prepared to find what we can do’ to help save the chain.
Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said nationalising Poundland would be ‘insane’.
He added: 'The hard truth is that in a dynamic economy, businesses are created, whilst others sadly fail. We cannot expect taxpayers to step in and solve all of life's problems.
‘Labour business policy is in chaos. When you get a government with so little business experience as this one, this is what results.’
Poundland is on the brink of collapse - putting 600 stores and 12,000 jobs at risk
Poundland, which was bought by private equity group Gordon Brothers for £1 last year, could crash into administration as early as this week – putting 600 stores and 12,000 jobs at risk in the run-up to Christmas.
A Poundland distribution centre employing 270 staff in Makerfield – Mr Burnham’s constituency in Greater Manchester – is also at risk.
Asked what his message was to Poundland owners and executives, the Prime Minister said: ‘Focus on the people in your employment.
‘Come up with a practical solution that saves jobs and saves those stores because many of them are viable propositions.
‘They’re on high streets. They matter in our communities. There is a solution to be found here. Sit down with us and let’s find it.’
Speaking to reporters while attending the Commonwealth Heads of Government meeting in Antigua, Mr Burnham acknowledged there was a limit to what ministers could do but he suggested there were ways forward for the firm.
‘There’s always a limit, but we’re prepared to to find what we can do,’ he said.
‘We believe in this instance there is a solution. There are many viable outlets here. Other retailers are expressing interest. Get around the table. Let’s find a solution.’
The comments came as Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds was set to meet US-based Gordon Brothers amid Government criticism of their handling of the retailer.
Business minister Kate Dearden is also due to hold talks with Poundland’s chief executive and chief finance officer.
Asked in the House of Lords if he could ‘rule out specific Poundland subsidy or nationalisation as a solution’, Lord Leong said: ‘The answer is no.’
He was later slapped down by departmental officials who said he had ‘misspoken’.
A Whitehall source added: 'There are no plans to nationalise Poundland.'
Company advisers are still in talks with parties interested in buying the brand and swathes of stores, around two months after a sale process was launched.
Tesco has held talks over proposals to buy up to 150 Poundland stores while Poundstretcher owner Fortress also showed its interest in purchasing as many as 250 shops.
It is understood that other grocery chains, such as Iceland and Lidl, are also in the frame to acquire some stores.
Wilko and The Range owner CDS Superstores and B&M have also expressed their interest in sites.
Downing Street has been critical of Gordon Brothers’ handling of the sale process.
‘It appears they’re not acting in the best interests of their loyal UK staff and stores,’ the Prime Minister’s official spokesman said.
It is an ‘extremely worrying situation for Poundland staff, their families and communities’ and the Government was staying close to the situation, the spokesman said.
‘Both the Prime Minister and the Business Secretary have been clear: they want to know what’s happening and Gordon Brothers need to explain why they haven’t accepted any offer to keep the company going.’
Gordon Brothers could also face questioning in Parliament over its actions.
Liam Byrne said the Commons Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee which he chairs has ‘issued a request to Gordon Brothers to come before us next week to answer questions’.
The crisis at Poundland has raised fresh questions over private equity ownership of household names across Britian’s high streets and beyond.
Other big firms taken over by private equity include struggling supermarket chains Asda and Morrisons.
Richard Walker, the boss of Iceland, accused Gordon Brothers of ‘private equity opportunism’ amid fears it would rather put Poundland into administration and sell off sites piecemeal than find a buyer to rescue the whole business.
He said: ‘You could say that it’s in my own interest to have one less competitor on the high street. But I say that we need our high streets to be places offering variety and vitality – with as many shops as we can sustain trading successfully, satisfying customers and providing good jobs.
‘Sure, it’s a tough market. As I’ve long argued, retail just gets harder and harder – not helped by government imposing more and more cost and complexity on businesses.
‘But Poundland isn’t bust. All the signs are that it’s been trading OK. Administration seems more about private equity opportunism than business necessity.
‘Good capitalism is about doing the right thing by our colleagues, customers and communities. Do that, and the profits follow.’
Bally Auluk, Usdaw national officer, said: 'This afternoon I am meeting with Employment Minister Kate Dearden, along with Poundland’s senior management team.
'We welcome the Government’s commitment to support our members and help to save jobs, including the Prime Minister’s statement today.
'We are aware that Poundland’s owners are set to meet with the Business Secretary, which is welcome, but we urge Gordon Brothers to engage directly with Usdaw as the trade union for Poundland staff, which they have so far refused to do.'

items.title: Don’t let Poundland owner maximise its return at our expense, suppliers say
items.summary: British companies that supply US-owned budget retailer face millions of pounds’ worth of losses if it collapses Suppliers facing millions of pounds in losses if Poundland collapses have said the chain’s US owner should not be permitted to maximise its return at their expense, as ministers attempt to intervene in the situation. The fate of the retail chain, its 12,000 staff and about 2,000 suppliers remains uncertain after it filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators at the high court last Thursday. Continue reading...
items.body:
Suppliers facing millions of pounds in losses if Poundland collapses have said the chain’s US owner should not be permitted to maximise its return at their expense, as ministers attempt to intervene in the situation.
The fate of the retail chain, its 12,000 staff and about 2,000 suppliers remains uncertain after it filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators at the high court last Thursday.
The US restructuring specialist Gordon Brothers, which bought the now 600-store Poundland chain for £1 last summer, remains in talks with at least two possible buyers for the company. They include Northern Ireland’s Martin Property Group, whose offer has been backed by the retailer’s management team.
Gordon Brothers executives are understood to be meeting Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, on Wednesday while Poundland’s management team have a separate meeting with Kate Dearden, the minister for the future of work, and the shop workers’ union Usdaw amid political pressure to find a rescue deal.
However, Gordon Brothers is understood to prefer the option to break up Poundland, sell off its stock and parcel up stores for sale to other retailers, including Tesco and the owner of Poundstretcher, because this would pay off more of a £30m shareholder loan.
This route could save some retail jobs but would leave suppliers with unpaid debts and millions of pounds’ worth of stock without a retailer to sell it to.
Karan Shah, a director of Universal Toiletries, a fragrance and toiletries supplier to Poundland, told the Guardian the company faced a financial risk of about £1.5m, including almost £700,000 in stock already delivered but yet to be paid for, and the rest in undelivered stock and components.
“Gordon Brothers should not be permitted to maximise its own financial return at the expense of suppliers without exploring all the alternatives of a solvent deal,” he said.
Shah suggested the timing of the potential administration appeared “very advantageous” to Gordon Brothers, “at the busiest time of year when the warehouses are full of stock”. This could leave millions of pounds’ worth of stock that could be sold off by any administrator to pay back the loans held by Gordon Brothers if Poundland is broken up.
Shah’s company worked with the chain for about a decade but stopped supplying stock in recent weeks amid concerns about payment. “We are unfortunately significantly exposed,” he said, adding that Poundland was its biggest UK client and “we are a family business, not a multinational that can afford to take a hit”.
Andrew Kay, the chief operating officer of the Oldham-based toy ball supplier John Leisure, said he would have to “rehome” more than a million products, many of which had already been manufactured and were in transit for next spring.
He said doing so would be difficult because many items had been made specifically for Poundland, and other retailers would not want the same sizes and quantities. “It is going to be a nightmare that will hurt me badly to deal with all that inventory,” he said.
While Kay has only a relatively small amount of stock for which he has yet to be paid sitting in Poundland, he said Gordon Brothers had questions to answer about its treatment of suppliers.
He felt the investment firm seemed to be “making money off the back of others” by attempting to put Poundland into administration at a time when it was filled with stock that had yet to be paid for.
He said Gordon Brothers’ aim to save stores and retail jobs by selling off groups of Poundland’s stores would not help suppliers.
Adam Turner, the sales director at the confectionery supplier Highcrest Retail Brands, based in Bradford, said he was set to lose millions of pounds in payments on stock the company had already supplied if the retailer went bust.
He said Highcrest had managed to find alternative buyers for some of its stock and had some insurance but was likely to lose out on payment for stock already provided and for investments in new products for Poundland. But “we can stomach it”, he said.
Shah, Turner and Kay said they were concerned about the future for their own suppliers if they missed out on Poundland orders. “This affects everyone in the supply chain,” Shah said. “Situations like this can wipe businesses out.”
It is estimated that Poundland’s collapse could affect up to 30,000 jobs when its supply chain is accounted for.
Gordon Brothers has been contacted for comment. It has previously said Poundland “faces multiple economic challenges, including rising inflation, increasing staffing costs and shrinkage from severe levels of shoplifting”.

items.body:
On 22 May 1987, retail history was made in Rotherham. Parkgate Retail World, thought at the time to be the UK’s largest open-air shopping centre, welcomed shoppers for some one-stop retail therapy. The official opening was marked in swanky fashion with a “breathtaking” display from Marlboro’s red-and-white branded biplanes, followed by a “spectacular” laser show, the first in South Yorkshire. Helen Worth – Coronation Street’s Gail Platt – cut the ribbon before jovial local people jostled to fill their car boots with goods from Comet, Jolly Giant and Poundstretcher.
Almost 40 years on, the razzle is a bit less dazzling. Parkgate, as the retail park is called now, looks like any large big-box outdoor shopping centre you might find on urban fringes. There’s a Primark, a Sports Direct and a Matalan, plus (of course) a Frankie & Benny’s. Shoppers still seem to love it. “I think it’s ideal. It’s got everything here,” says Robert Gordon. The 66-year-old retired factory production manager had popped to Pets at Home to get a cupcake and toy for his dog Bruno’s fourth birthday.
Gordon has lived in Rotherham for 24 years. “A lot of people come to outlets like this. It’s very rare we go into the town centre and, if we did, we’d go to Sheffield,” he says. He is hardly an outlier. Almost half of Britons don’t visit their high street weekly. Instead, shoppers are opting for retail parks. Business is so strong, retailers are scrambling for spots, even paying extra to secure their place. By the end of 2025, only 4.8% of retail park lots in Britain were vacant, according to real estate consultancy Knight Frank – the lowest level on record. Vacancy rates for UK high streets, on the other hand, sit at 13%, reports Savills.
Gordon remembers a time two decades ago when you “couldn’t move” in Rotherham town centre, especially at the weekend. “It was packed and all the local shops were busy. Now these big outlets have taken over.” He admits his shopping habits come at a cost to the local community. “We are part of the problem,” he says. “It’s not progress. You used to meet people, but now you’re lucky to see anyone you know. Most people will come here and shop, get what they need and go back home.”
Jo Hill, 59, and her husband Richard, 65, are also Rotherham locals. Until recently, they hadn’t set foot in the town centre in nearly two decades. “What you see is either vape shops, nail shops or charity shops,” says Jo, who is semi-retired. Rotherham town centre is bookended by Parkgate at one end, and Meadowhall – one of the UK’s largest indoor shopping centres – at the other. The couple were visiting Parkgate to buy a printer from Currys. “For the big stuff, it’s either here or Meadowhall,” says Richard.
A short journey away, in Rotherham town centre, the picture is different. About 70 retail units, 24% overall, are vacant, far higher than the national average, and it is immediately apparent. One of the first things you see when leaving the train station is a derelict branch of BrightHouse, a rent-to-own retailer selling large appliances and furniture, which shut down in 2020. Further up is an anonymous-looking shopfront with smashed windows, graffiti and empty panelling where a shop sign should be – another shuttered chain, Fultons Foods, which closed in 2022. The only identifying mark is a window sticker: “There’s always change at Fultons.” Vape shops, discount chains and charity shops dominate the street.
The arrival of Parkgate Retail World nearly four decades ago wasn’t without friction. Even then, market traders expressed fears about the impact on business and, in Westminster, parliamentarians warned that these mini shopping metropolises would drain jobs from the high street, “disembowel towns and villages” and disadvantage those unable to drive.
Donna, who owns a furniture shop, and Saj, who runs a sandwich deli, are on their lunch break when I stop them. “It’s declined totally. I really wish it hasn’t, but it has,” says Donna. Nowadays she usually serves about four or five customers, and her daily takings have declined to “virtually nothing”, she says. Saj agrees that footfall is nonexistent.
The pair say safety is one reason that locals, especially elderly people, are staying home. “People have had their bags stolen, or been followed into banks; you’re watched when using the cash machines,” says Donna. “People will only come if they feel safe. It was always the older generation that came into the shop buying beds. Now their families won’t let them come out.” In 2023, a government analysis found that the number of crimes carried out per 1,000 people in Rotherham town was 160, 72% higher than the national average at the time. Recent police data shows there were 1,105 crimes, including 356 violent and sexual offences and 188 instances of shoplifting recorded in central Rotherham in August of this year alone. Nearby Sheffield city centre recorded 836 crimes in the same period. Donna says drug users also hang around her shopfront. “They sleep in my doorway sometimes. There’s needles and all sorts left. We’re not getting anybody into the shop because it looks bad.”
For Saj, the lack of affordable parking is another problem killing the high street. Car ownership has soared since the advent of the retail park. In 1971, 52% of households in Britain owned a car. A decade later, this had jumped to 60%, and by 2022 nearly three-quarters of households had a car. On its website, Parkgate touts its “over 2,000 free parking spaces”, all in one concentrated area.
Within Rotherham town centre, there are 1,610 spaces, which, until fairly recently, were all paid – though the council has recognised parking as a challenge. In 2016 it cut long-stay charges from £6.50 to £3.50 a day, and last year, it introduced free parking for one hour on weekdays. At the weekend, some spaces are free all day, but many, while acknowledging the council’s efforts, say it is not enough.
Sitting on a bench and lapping up the sun on Rotherham High Street are Leo Lopez and Claire Mercer. “I’ve seen a massive change,” says 50-year-old Lopez, a support worker. Mercer, also 50, a road safety campaigner, agrees. “You don’t come here to do general shopping after 3.30pm. It’s aggro caused by drugs mainly. People are more out of their head by that time. It’s an unfortunate truth, but it’s everywhere.”
The state of the town centre “deteriorates the morale”, says Lopez. And it may be contributing to the rise of rightwing populism: research by the thinktank Power to Change published last year found higher support for Reform UK in areas with run-down high streets that have high vacancy rates. Mercer says a part of town filled with ethnic minority shops and restaurants has been disparaged by some as “a foreign bazaar”. “Would they prefer the shops were empty? It’s much better to have busy shops, but people don’t like change.”
The town centre isn’t totally devoid of good news. Days before I came to town, Yella Brick Road – a quirky clothing and homewares shop – was preparing to close its doors, a decision it reversed after loyal shoppers flocked to keep the business afloat. Owner Dannii Paston has been trading in the town centre for 17 years. “Recently, people are just careful with money. We’re a shop where you don’t need anything in here – it’s all treat spends,” she says.
Surprisingly, it was the relocation of Primark, the supposed big, bad clothing behemoth, that Paston believes cost her the most business. “I didn’t think they were our customers, but actually, people would go to Primark for certain things like pants, tights or a cheap dress for the 10-year-old, then come to us for themselves,” she says. Even when the chains were in the town centre, their limited stock couldn’t compete with their warehouse-sized counterparts in Parkgate, says Paston. “It’s a societal shift on how people want to shop. Why would you go into a tiny high-street shop that’s got a quarter of the selection?
She believes supermarkets were the first to pull customers from town. In many large Morrisons branches, for example, you can take your passport photo, wash your clothes in an on-site launderette and even have keys cut while doing the weekly shop. Sainsbury’s has closed 420 Argos high-street shops since 2020, after acquiring its parent company, and shifted them inside its larger stores. “It’s like a little high street,” says Paston.
The out-of-town shopping destination – whether it’s a retail park, mall or outlet – hasn’t always been part of British life. The UK’s first such complex, Gem Superstore, opened in West Bridgford, Nottingham in 1964. Operated by an American company, Government Employees Mart, it brought US-style shopping to Britain – and demand was through the roof. The Goldfinger star Shirley Eaton was brought in for the official opening day, when 30,000 people rushed down its aisles. At 110,000 sq ft, fairly paltry compared with the sprawling shopping complexes that followed, it was more akin to a modern-day large supermarket. Two years later, Asda, then still a fledgling chain of small grocers, bought the site for its first superstore.
London’s Brent Cross Shopping Centre, which opened in 1976, took things to the next level. Traders feared that the 800,000 sq ft behemoth – boasting air conditioning (unheard of at the time) and the triple threat of Fenwick, John Lewis and Marks & Spencer under the same roof – would hammer local trade, and the Labour government tried to thwart the development. But Barnet council, in a Tory stronghold where Margaret Thatcher held her parliamentary seat, gave it the enthusiastic thumbs up. The indoor shopping centre opened the year after Thatcher’s ascendancy to leader of the opposition in 1975. Already there was consensus among local authorities that out-of-town shopping centres would destroy high streets but, after the Tories entered Downing Street in 1979, planning rules were eased. “There is a change of attitude in the 1980s which begins to allow these out-of-town locations,” says Alistair Kefford, the chair of urban studies at Leiden University in the Netherlands. In 1981, there was one out-of-town retail park in the UK. By 1988, there were 90 and at the end of 1996, there were 385.
In the end, the critics were right. “There’s only a certain level of consumer demand within a regional economy,” says Kefford. “If you build a wonderful, shiny, exciting new shopping mall or retail park, it doesn’t create a lot of new shoppers. They just stop going somewhere else.”
The bruising figures bear this out. In 2024, 13,479 shops across the UK closed their doors. While retail accounts for 5% of the UK economy and less than a tenth of employment, an area’s former glory is often starkly highlighted by its decrepit high street. “Dying high streets make people feel ashamed of their place, that their life is falling apart,” says Eddie Blake, a director at the architecture practice Studio Weave.
How to save the high street has become fertile political territory. Parkgate lies within John Healey’s constituency. In 2019, the now-chancellor scolded M&S for shutting its branch in the shopping complex, about a decade after relocating from Rotherham town centre, meaning the retailer would “disappear from the town for the first time in 125 years”. Since entering No 11, Healey has said “blighted” high streets will soon be “on the up”. Last month, Andy Burnham announced £210m in funding to regenerate down-on-their-luck high streets. But Kefford is sceptical. “Retail is a barometer – it’s not an engine. Where you see retail doing well, it’s a sign that the regional economy itself is doing well, but retail by itself won’t make a place wealthy. It’s not an engine of growth because it relies on people spending their disposable income,” he says.
Efforts to turn the ship can often be futile. “Once a location has set off down a particular path, it’s very hard to get out of it. In fact, everything leads further and further down that path. The narrowing range of shops, the growth of empty properties – these are things that snowball and get worse and worse,” says Kefford.
So, are UK high streets doomed? Shops “are probably not going to come back”, says Kefford, but there’s still hope. “In the 1950s and 1960s, town centres sustained loads of uses. There were many more houses and social activities: churches, working men’s clubs, community associations, charities, theatres. We need to think more fundamentally and creatively about what is the point of a town centre,” he says.
This may be good for society, too. Blake says the retail parks and shopping centres, and the cars we use to get to them, contribute to an “atomised culture that makes people feel alone”. A multifunction high street can better facilitate social interaction: “The small-grain interactions of social life are better, higher quality, and more frequent.”
Until then, many of us will be drawn to these bland, uninspiring shopping pens on the fringes of town. On my way to the train station, the No 8 bus pulls up on the high street, having just stopped at Parkgate. Sure enough, the passengers who alight are carrying bags from Primark, TK Maxx and Sports Direct.

items.body:
The chief executive of Marks & Spencer has called John Healey’s first budget as chancellor a “whole lot of nothing” and bemoaned an “onslaught of taxation and regulation” from the Labour government despite welcoming an expected deal on EU border checks.
Stuart Machin said he was disappointed at last week’s budget statement, adding that it “didn’t really address the issues we need to focus on growth”. He said the chancellor’s “real terms” freeze on business rates, for example, would lead to an additional £10m on M&S’s existing £170m rates bill.
Machin also criticised plans for the “most ridiculous” deposit return scheme under which retailers must install machines for the return of cans and plastic bottles in stores in England and Scotland from next October in order to drive up recycling rates. In Wales, the scheme is to also include glass bottles.
The M&S boss said he was “very supportive” of a new food trade deal between the UK and EU, which is expected to be completed later this month. Machin said this would help reduce a £10m post-Brexit hit to the retailer caused by the paperwork, packaging and logistical costs involved in sending goods to the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland. He added that the deal would also help UK exports of food to mainland Europe.
The comments emerged as M&S said a sustained cyber-attack that forced it to shut down its website last year had continued to hurt clothing sales over the past summer.
The retailer said profits bounced back to a better-than-expected £355m in the six months to 26 September from only £3.4m a year before, as it partly recovered from the hack. The attack, which began over Easter 2025, forced M&S to shut its website, which sells clothing and homewares, for more than six weeks.
Total sales over the half year across the food to fashion group rose 16.2% to £9.2bn.
M&S said sales and profit from its clothing and homewares arm remained below that of two years ago as “availability was constrained due to the longer-than-expected impact of manual ordering processes following the incident, while profitability was diluted by an increased mix of online sales, which have higher fulfilment costs”.
The retailer has previously explained that its team of buyers had to calculate demand and make orders to suppliers without the help of their usual technology and detailed information last year.
Machin said: “We are broadening our appeal and the brand is in good health, but the results fell short of their potential and show there is a lot more to do.”
He added that the manual ordering meant that in some clothing categories M&S did not stock enough everyday products, such as denim and knitwear, over the summer. Profits were also hit by more people shopping online during the “long hot summer”.
Machin said the impact of the cyber-attack “lasted longer than we expected”, but added: “That’s now behind us.”
M&S said it had been able to take its biggest ever share of a declining clothing market despite the availability problems, which were now resolved but added: “Market conditions remain challenging.”
Machin said the UK clothing market was down by 11%, with £1bn in clothing sales lost across the industry in the last six months as the hot weather, low consumer confidence and a shift away from spending on nonessentials hit sales.
He added that the industry was still “heavily discounting” and M&S was trying to avoid that trend by pricing its goods affordably.
M&S clothing, beauty and homewares sales rose 17.5% to almost £2bn in the half year compared with the same period last year, which was affected by the hack.
Performance is expected to improve in the second half as M&S said availability has now recovered “creating a better balance between core and seasonal stock”.
Its food business powered ahead, increasing sales by almost 14% to £5.2bn in the half year as it opened seven new stores and expanded or refurbished others.
The group’s Ocado joint venture also swung to a half-year profit of £25.6m from a loss of £3.1m a year before as sales rose 16% and it improved the efficiency of its deliveries
M&S said it expected to cut £120m in costs this year across technology, logistics and stores. Machin said the retailer would not be making redundancies but was likely to be cautious on hiring new workers as it tried to offset new costs, including £35m related to a new packaging levy.

items.title: M&S boss accuses Labour of 'biggest tax grab in history' after an 'onslaught' of cost increases
items.summary: The boss of Marks & Spencer has accused the Government of staging one of the 'biggest tax grabs in history'.
items.body:
M&S boss accuses Labour of 'biggest tax grab in history' after an 'onslaught' of cost increases
The boss of Marks & Spencer has accused the Government of staging one of the 'biggest tax grabs in history' as it was left reeling from a series of cost increases.
Boss Stuart Machin said the retailer had been hit by an 'onslaught' of headwinds in recent months, and that its business rates bill would rise by another £10 million next year.
Writing in the Mail last month, Machin called on the Chancellor to reverse 'the mistakes of the last two Budgets' and said rises to employer National Insurance contributions had made it harder for firms to hire young people.
Today he dismissed John Healey's Budget as a 'whole lot of nothing' and said the past three years of Labour policies equate to 'one of the biggest tax grabs in history'.
'You can't ignore the onslaught of all the headwinds,' he said. 'It's probably more challenging than we've ever seen in the past in trying to balance the books. But we do want to make sure we're constantly getting costs out and reinvesting in value.'
M&S paid out £40million for the new packaging tax from its food margin, which 'really just meant in that month we broke even on food.'
And while the extra costs don't equate to redundancies, Machin said the retailer has to be 'mindful of future recruitment costs'.
But Marks & Spencer says it is primed for an ‘unforgettable’ Christmas as profits recovered after last year’s cyber attack.
Marks & Spencer boss Stuart Machin said the Budget had been a 'whole lot of nothing'.
Profits rebounded to £355.1million for the 26 weeks to September 26, compared to £3.4million last year after M&S was forced to pause sales on its website for around six weeks after cyber criminals infiltrated its systems over the Easter weekend in 2025.
Sales in its food business rose 13.9 per cent to £5.1billion as boss Stuart Machin said the retailer was gearing up to cash in on customers dining out less and ordering fewer takeaways this Christmas.
The business has also seen momentum behind new food ranges after its product development director Kathryn Turner has become a beloved star of social media in recent weeks.
Machin said he was 'monitoring' incidents of supermarkets' fridges being hacked in Europe closely and that cyber security is a concern 'every day' for the company.
But M&S said its fashion, home and beauty business had faced the ‘long tail impact’ of the hack, resulting in disruption to availability ‘in selected core lines and sizes’.
Sales recovered 17.5 per cent to just under £2billion compared to last year, but fell short of recovering to its 2024 levels.
Machin has previously said some traditional customers of the brand have complained about the lack of options for their demographic and asked for fewer ‘skimpy tops’.
He said that some had complained about there not being enough summer dresses with sleeves while viral products sold out too quickly, leaving Machin to admit 'we felt we left money on the table'.
Machin said the segment had been ‘gaining share in a declining market’, claiming that Worldpanel research shows £1billion of sales have come out of the UK fashion market over the six months, compared with the level two years earlier.
He added: ‘Availability and stock flow are now improving, we are broadening our appeal and the brand is in good health, but the results fell short of their potential and show there is a lot more to do.’
The high street boss acknowledged that customers were worried about the cost of living, but research showed 'they're saving a bit [to get] ready for Christmas'.
He added: ‘So we're not overly concerned with Christmas. We know customers are telling us they're eating out less. That's good for us. We know customers are saying they're buying nest takeaways. That's good for us. That gives us a bit of confidence as we head into Christmas.’
It comes as the FTSE 100 store has recruited Lucy Punch, star of the sitcom Amandaland, as the face of its Christmas advertising campaign.

items.title: David Jones expected to fall into administration after failed 11th hour talks with biggest landlord
items.summary: Future of 188-year-old department store hangs in balance after no agreement was struck with Westfield owner Scentre Group Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast David Jones is poised to fall into administration after 11th-hour talks between its private equity owner and primary landlord broke down, putting the future of the 188-year-old upmarket department store chain at risk. The upheaval follows years of steep losses, weak consumer spending and a string of underperforming stores that left the heritage retailer defaulting on its rent. Continue reading...
items.body:
David Jones is poised to fall into administration after 11th-hour talks between its private equity owner and primary landlord broke down, putting the future of the 188-year-old upmarket department store chain at risk.
The upheaval follows years of steep losses, weak consumer spending and a string of underperforming stores that left the heritage retailer defaulting on its rent.
Its main landlord, Scentre Group, which owns Westfield, said discussions with David Jones’s owner, Anchorage Capital Partners, had ended without an agreement.
“They have not paid rent since September and therefore are in breach,” Scentre’s chief executive, Elliott Rusanow, said in a statement on Wednesday.
“We have made a generous offer to Anchorage Capital Partners that would have facilitated the continuation of David Jones trading and that offer has disappointingly been rejected by them.”
Two people with knowledge of the discussions but unauthorised to speak publicly said the next step was for administrators to be appointed.
While an administration process could help David Jones overhaul its business, it also takes the retailer’s fate out of its own hands, with the retailer subject to the competing claims of creditors.
Administrators would want to keep stores trading with little interruption through Black Friday and Christmas to capture the vital cash injection during those popular trading periods, one person briefed on the matter said.
Earlier on Wednesday, a David Jones spokesperson said its chief executive, Erica Berchtold, was in advanced discussions with key stakeholders.
“This includes a review of the portfolio of stores across Australia and the trading terms with suppliers and brand partners,” the spokesperson said in a statement.
The retailer was contacted for comment after Scentre confirmed that talks had ended.
David Jones had been seeking to renegotiate lease terms with its landlords and reduce its store numbers from the current 38, aiming to offload poor performing suburban sites, according to a person with knowledge of discussions.
Longer term, the retailer had wanted to reduce its network to about one-third of its current size.
While mid- to upmarket department stores have been struggling for years, the re-emergence of high inflation and the associated cost-of-living pressures has made trading conditions even worse.
Shares in Myer Holdings, operator of the rival Myer department store chain, are down more than 50% in 2026.
RMIT University advertising expert, Prof Robert Crawford, said David Jones had been caught in an intensifying squeeze between discount chains and luxury fashion houses that sell direct to consumers.
“The David Jones model has really struggled to adapt to modern retailing,” Crawford said.

items.title: Primark lacks fizz as it approaches its go-it-alone moment
items.summary: After a profits dip, the chain’s demerger from its sister food company still makes sense but is unlikely to reveal tons of value Primark brings forward home deliveries plan by two years as profits slide The business logic for demerging Primark from Associated British Foods’ greater Ovaltine-to-Twinings empire – an event due to happen by the end of next year – is impeccable. Read this year’s results statement and you wonder why the controlling Weston family took 20 years to get behind the idea. One paragraph can be about a yeast plant in India or the impact of high gas prices on sugar-refining margins; the next can jump to Primark’s new “digital flywheel” or the progress of the “By Coleen” collection. Even by conglomerate standards, food staples and discount fashion has always been an odd mix. Separating into two FTSE 100 companies, with stand-alone governance, makes sense. Continue reading...
items.body:
The business logic for demerging Primark from Associated British Foods’ greater Ovaltine-to-Twinings empire – an event due to happen by the end of next year – is impeccable. Read this year’s results statement and you wonder why the controlling Weston family took 20 years to get behind the idea.
One paragraph can be about a yeast plant in India or the impact of high gas prices on sugar-refining margins; the next can jump to Primark’s new “digital flywheel” or the progress of the “By Coleen” collection. Even by conglomerate standards, food staples and discount fashion has always been an odd mix. Separating into two FTSE 100 companies, with stand-alone governance, makes sense.
But it would be hard to say the rejig will reveal tons of value, another reason conglomerates often give for doing the splits. Primark obviously isn’t a hidden jewel because it already makes two-thirds of the group profit – and it isn’t currently on sparkling form either.
Or, at least, it’s not in continental Europe. A like-for-like sales decline there of 4.7% for the financial year is jarring even in the context of “weak” consumer sentiment. The way ABF tells it, the continental operation is simply a year or so behind the refresh treatment that has been administered on the UK stores. We’re talking sharper digital marketing campaigns, a rejig of ranges, the introduction of click & collect and so on.
The trouble is, the same explanation was given in January, when the gap between the home performance and that on the continent became apparent. Ten months later, the story remains largely the same. The UK and Ireland are in positive like-for-like sales territory (of 0.5%) but the continent is still miles off. Market conditions in Germany, Italy and Spain were all described as “very challenging”.
Since Britain is now the priority for a home delivery service to capture “incremental” shoppers, one can imagine the gap will remain wide for some time yet. Perhaps online-only operators such as Shein, Temu and Zalando are simply more of a headache on the continent.
None of which alters the underlying strength of the Primark machine. Never mind the U-turn on the economics of home delivery, there are still physical stores being opened, including in the US. This is still a formidable operation with almost £10bn of annual turnover.
But the potential for profit growth tends to be a metric would-be new investors in newly liberated companies look at.
On operating profits, Primark stayed above £1bn (just) for the year, but the number was 11% down on a year ago. For this year, the forecast is for a same-again profit margin of 10%-ish. There is a sense, even while opening new stores, of working hard to go roughly sideways.
No new money will be raised in next year’s demerger, so timing is irrelevant in one sense. Shareholders will get what they already own, just in two parts; there will be no real need for investment banking hype.
All the same, the overall ABF, as currently constituted, is forecasting a second year in a row of lower earnings because the food ingredients side, especially sugar, is still sticky. Meanwhile, the £1.9bn of share buy-backs over the past four years have come to an end as the group is in long-term investment mode.
There could be another 12 months until the big split, which allows time for things to perk up. But in current “macroeconomic headwinds” conditions, ABF is travelling slowly to the historic separation. It’s still the right thing to do – just don’t expect fireworks.

items.title: Protect Poundland from predatory capitalism, MPs tell government
items.summary: Budget retailer and 12,000 jobs at risk after US owner fails to accept buyout offers MPs have called on the government to protect Poundland and other high street stores from “predatory capitalism” and asset-stripping. The fate of the retail chain and its 12,000 staff remains uncertain after it filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators at the high court last Thursday. Continue reading...
items.body:
MPs have called on the government to protect Poundland and other high street stores from “predatory capitalism” and asset-stripping.
The fate of the retail chain and its 12,000 staff remains uncertain after it filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators at the high court last Thursday.
The board of Poundland has lined up the advisory company AlixPartners to run the process after the owner, US restructuring specialist Gordon Brothers, ceased providing funding.
In an urgent question in the House of Commons on Tuesday, Gareth Snell, Labour MP for Stoke-on-Trent Central, asked the government what could be done to “send a message to Gordon Brothers that the predatory capitalism that they are putting into this company will not be tolerated, because we in this country will always stand with people before profit”.
Another Labour MP, Antonia Bance, asked what measures the government would use to “hold Gordon Brothers to account”, and if it would “establish an urgent review of whether our corporate governance and insolvency frameworks give sufficient protection against asset stripping and short term financial engineering, at the cost of jobs and our high streets?”
The Green party MP Hannah Spencer said the “scandal” of Poundland “exposes a very serious problem, that our economy is vulnerable to private equity vultures who swoop in and prey on our high street brands by loading them with debt and then trying to ditch them for a profit”.
Kate Dearden, the minister for the future of work, told parliament that government officials had held talks with Gordon Brothers on Monday night and she would meet Poundland’s management team along with Usdaw, the shop workers’ union, on Wednesday.
She said Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, would meet Gordon Brothers again later this week as political pressure mounts on the company to accept a solvent bid for Poundland.
Liam Byrne, the chair of business select committee, has also asked Gordon Brothers to answer its questions about Poundland on Wednesday next week.
Dearden said the government could not involve itself in the “commercial negotiations” with potential buyers or comment on individual bids.
However, she said the government was “taking a responsible approach not to sit by and do nothing” and was putting pressure on Gordon Brothers to accept it had “responsibilities as well as rights” over Poundland and its employees.
Gordon Brothers is understood to remain in talks with at least two potential buyers for the whole company, including a fully funded offer from Northern Ireland’s Martin Property Group.
Another offer from Innovest, an investment group understood to be advised by former Reform election candidate Charles Bunker, is believed to have partial funding in place.
The chance of Poundland avoiding mass store closures and job losses is shrinking by the day because suppliers have held back on deliveries, hurting its ability to trade.
Gordon Brothers is believed to be unwilling to accept Martin Property’s offer of about £15m, only half of which would be paid immediately, because it falls short of repaying a £30m shareholder loan.
The prime minister’s spokesperson said: “We continue to stay close to what’s an extremely worrying situation for Poundland staff, their families and communities.
“Gordon Brothers need to explain why they haven’t accepted any offer to keep the company going. That’s the case. It appears they’re not acting in the best interests of their loyal UK staff and stores.”
In a letter to the government, reported by Sky News, Gordon Brothers executive Mark Newton-Jones defended its approach, saying it had “supported Poundland with £85m of additional financing” since acquiring it for £1 last year and the chain had returned to underlying profit.
However, the letter added: “Like other high street retailers, the company faces multiple economic challenges, including rising inflation, increasing staffing costs and shrinkage from severe levels of shoplifting, which means it is still not cash-generative at a sustainable level despite the turnaround efforts.”
Dozens of MPs from around the UK have called on the government to reassure their constituents that action would be taken to stop Poundland’s collapse.
Bradley Thomas, the Conservative party business spokesperson, blamed the government for Poundland’s demise. He said: “The current economic landscape is hostile to British business.”
Earlier on Tuesday, the founder of Poundland, Steve Smith, told the Guardian that staff at the chain could be out of work for years if it collapsed.
Gordon Brothers was approached for comment.

items.title: Primark brings forward home deliveries plan by two years as profits slide
items.summary: Retailer acquires robot-assisted warehouse and intends to have UK service up and running before end of 2027 Primark is to begin making home deliveries by the end of next year as it aims to win new shoppers after a slide in profits. George Weston, the boss of the cut-price fashion chain’s owner Associated British Foods (ABF), said it had brought forward the launch of Primark’s home delivery plans by about two years. Continue reading...
items.body:
Primark is to begin making home deliveries by the end of next year as it aims to win new shoppers after a slide in profits.
George Weston, the boss of the cut-price fashion chain’s owner Associated British Foods (ABF), said it had brought forward the launch of Primark’s home delivery plans by about two years.
The company was able to speed up the process by snapping up a robot-assisted warehouse in Sheffield from Debenhams, the owner of Boohoo, PrettyLittle Thing and Karen Millen.
Primark will take over the warehouse by the middle of next year and is working on preparing its suppliers to provide stock suitable for sending out to individual shoppers as well as the usual bulk orders for stores.
Primark already offers a click and collect service in the UK which it has gradually rolled out since 2022. The service is not available to its stores in mainland Europe.
The chain, which has 511 stores across 21 countries, will launch home deliveries in the UK by December next year. It intends to offer the service in mainland Europe after that, but has not set out a timeframe.
Primark has previously said it could not make money by selling fashion for home delivery, but Weston said the economics had changed with delivery and returns charges that could cover most of the logistical costs now common across the industry.
He added that the group’s research had shown it could attract new customers, rather than just substituting a sale in store for a less profitable one online.
“We now know there’s a group of shoppers who don’t reject Primark but just don’t use us very often as they are too far away from a store or prefer to shop online,” he said.
The move comes as Primark faces tough competition from the rise of cut-price online specialists such as Shein as well as the supermarkets’ clothing ranges and the likes of H&M and Zara, all of which sell online and in stores.
Weston insisted that Shein was not grabbing more than a “little bit” of market share from Primark, and that there was more competition from those who could mix online and stores.
Sales at Primark rose 4% to £9.8bn in the year to 12 September led by new store openings. Sales at established UK stores rose just 0.5% and sales at established stores in mainland Europe slumped 4.7% and in the US were down 2.6% as shoppers reined in spending on clothing amid higher energy and fuel bills.
Primark said performance in the UK had been helped by improved ranges, action to cut prices and more marketing, tactics that are now being rolled out across Europe. However, that action saw profits drop 10% to £1bn.
ABF intends to spin off Primark in December 2027, separating it from its sugar and food business that includes brands such as Twinings teas, Blue Dragon flavourings and Jordans cereals.

items.title: Asda hires ex-Morrisons boss in bid to grow firm
items.summary: David Potts takes charge of Asda, which is based in Leeds, with immediate effect.
items.body:
Asda hires ex-Morrisons boss in bid to grow firm
- Published
Asda has appointed a former Morrisons boss as chief executive to help lead revival efforts at the supermarket chain.
Asda, which is based in Leeds, said David Potts would take on the role with immediate effect, while current boss Allan Leighton would become non-executive chairman, two years after returning to lead the supermarket chain.
Potts led Morrisons from its Bradford headquarters for eight years until 2023, overseeing a turnaround during which the supermarket chain was bought by US private equity firm Clayton, Dubilier & Rice.
Potts said Asda had "made good progress but significant opportunities remain" to reinvigorate sales, with a focus on keeping prices low for shoppers.
"By making improvements to the shopping trip every week, which customers can experience and feel in their pockets, we will revitalise the business and bring benefits for all our stakeholders, including our 116,296 very hard-working colleagues," he said.
Before joining Morrisons, Potts was chief executive of Tesco's Irish business, its UK arm and its Asian operation.
According to Asda, Leighton had planned to step aside from the day-to-day running of the group, after he returned in 2024, more than two decades after serving as chief executive.
"Over the last two years, we have stabilised the business and returned it to some growth," said Leighton.
"David has an outstanding record in our industry, his experience is exactly what we now require for the next stage of our transformation and beyond and it will be great to work with him."
Last year, issues with an IT upgrade hit product availability at the supermarket and dented sales, impacting its bottom line.
But in August, it reported sales had returned to growth for the current quarter for the first time in two years.

items.title: Jeremy Clarkson's 1996 Ferrari he described as 'the greatest car in the world, ever' set to sell for £250,000
items.summary: Despite waxing lyrical about its engine and showering praise on its road manners, the petrolhead-turned-farmer kept it for only four years before giving it away as a competition prize.
items.body:
Jeremy Clarkson's 1996 Ferrari he described as 'the greatest car in the world, ever' set to sell for £250,000
If there's one person's opinion on a car that motorists trust, it's Jeremy Clarkson's.
And a Ferrari the former Top Gear and The Grand Tour host bought after declaring it 'the greatest car in the world, ever' and the 'nicest car I have ever, ever driven' is heading to auction later this month.
Clarkson purchased the 1996 Ferrari F355 GTS after being blown away by its performance during a road test for the BBC motoring show that made him famous.
It would have cost him around £95,000 at the time, the equivalent of almost £200,000 today when adjusted for inflation.
But despite waxing lyrical about its engine and showering praise on its road manners, the petrolhead-turned-farmer kept it for only four years before giving it away as a competition prize.
Now it could be yours... if you have deep enough pockets.
Jezza's Fezza is heading to the auction block in Birmingham on Saturday, November 14 with a guide price of between £200,000 and £250,000 – a higher price than it was offered to collectors just over a year ago.
The value of the F355 GTS appears to have received a boost from the recent surge in classic Ferrari prices, which have shot up following a number of record sales in early 2026.
This 1996 Ferrari F355 GTB was bought new by Jeremy Clarkson, who documented the purchase process in a Top Gear episode. Now it's heading to auction...
The mid-engined supercar, powered by a 380bhp 3.5-litre V8 engine mated to a six-speed manual gearbox, is widely recognised as one of Ferrari's greatest hits of the Nineties.
Registration P199 YPL combines extensively documented Clarkson provenance with desirable options, including rare factory sports seats and the GTS targa-style removable roof, and has covered 15,241 miles from new.
Delivered through Maranello Sales in Egham in August 1996, Clarkson's order followed a very public deliberation over colour.
He initially considered green on the basis that everyone else chose red before eventually ordering the car in Rosso Corsa.
He specified Crema leather upholstery, Rosso carpets and carbon-backed sports seats finished in Crema with red inserts.
The Ferrari featured regularly in his Sunday Times columns, including when he retook, and failed, his driving test in May 1999.
But in 2000, after covering around 6,000 miles, he gave it away as a reader prize having conceded that he'd bought the wrong model (he should have chosen the coupe), the wrong colour, and coming to the conclusion that 'you can't really go anywhere in a car like this'.
In his Top Gear segment, he states: 'You get stopped by the police constantly. If you leave it on the street, people spit in it. And if you leave it at home, the battery goes flat. It's useless!'
Despite waxing lyrical about its engine and showering praise on its road manners, the petrolhead-turned-farmer kept it for four years before giving it away as a competition prize
In his Top Gear segment, he states: 'You get stopped by the police constantly. If you leave it on the street, people spit in it. And if you leave it at home, the battery goes flat. It's useless!'
The winner kept the car for three years before selling it in 2003. It was then retained by its third owner for a decade until 2013 and has changed hands since.
It will go under the hammer at Iconic Auctioneers' NEC Classic Motor Show Sale in less than a fortnight's time, alongside three models from Clarkson's private collection that appeared on The Grand Tour.
However, eagle-eyed classic car enthusiasts will notice the estimate represents a significant increase in value compared to a year ago.
The same Ferrari was offered at RM Sotheby's sale at Cliveden House in Buckinghamshire in July 2025 with a guide price of between £180,000 and £220,000.
Even then, it failed to find a buyer and was subsequently offered to collectors for £190,000 or nearest offer.
Registration P199 YPL combines extensively documented Clarkson provenance with desirable options and has covered 15,241 miles from new
Clarkson's Ferrari was offered at auction a year ago with a lower guide price and didn't sell. However, cars from the Italian marque's Nineties era have soared in value in 2026
The value of analogue Ferraris from the 1980s-2000s have surged in value in 2026 after a number of high-profile sales at record prices
However, a recent surge in values of collectible Ferraris has swept through the classic car market.
The trend was triggered by record sales of five halo models from the famous Italian marque in January, sending prices into overdrive.
Values of modern classic Ferraris are said to have almost tripled overnight, with owners looking to cash in on growing demand for Eighties, Nineties and Noughties-era cars with large-capacity engines and manual gearboxes.
The Ferrari lot includes Clarkson's original order correspondence and the warranty card naming him as the car's first owner, which should only bolster its collectability.
Introduced in 1994, the F355 represented a substantial advancement over the outgoing 348.
Its 3.5-litre V8 used five valves per cylinder to produce 380bhp at 8,250rpm, delivering a 0-62mph sprint in 4.7 seconds and a top speed in excess of 180mph.
Harry Fox-Edwards, car specialist at Iconic Auctioneers, said: 'Many enthusiasts will remember Jeremy's enthusiasm for the F355, and this is the car he bought for himself.
'The original correspondence and ownership documents give that story real substance. Its mileage, manual gearbox and rare sports seats make it a particularly appealing Ferrari.
'Finding cars with character and a history worth telling is a great part of what we do, whether that's a Ferrari of this calibre or someone's first classic.'

items.body:
Brent crude slides 3% after Trump says US will stop military funding to Israel after year end
Brent crude has turned negative, sliding 3%, after Donald Trump said the US will stop providing military funding to Israel after the end of this year.
The US president said he made a deal with Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and that Washington would no longer be providing military aid to Israel after the end of this year.
Speaking to Fox News’ Fox and Friends programme, Trump said Israel no longer needs it and that some Democrats and left-wing politicians were using this US funding to Israel as a talking point to criticise Republicans.
Now, as far as paying Israel, Bibi Netanyahu and I have made a deal that we give Israel $4bn a year, and we made a deal months ago that we’re stopping.
We’ve already agreed that by the end of this year we won’t be paying Israel. Now we’ll help Israel if they need it.
