The US president said he made a deal with Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and that Washington would no longer be providing military aid to Israel after the end of this year.
Speaking to Fox News’ Fox and Friends programme, Trump said Israel no longer needs it and that some Democrats and left-wing politicians were using this US funding to Israel as a talking point to criticise Republicans.
Now, as far as paying Israel, Bibi Netanyahu and I have made a deal that we give Israel $4bn a year, and we made a deal months ago that we’re stopping.
We’ve already agreed that by the end of this year we won’t be paying Israel. Now we’ll help Israel if they need it.
Hannah Spencer, Green MP for Gordon and Denton, described Gordon Brothers, the owner of Poundland, as “private equity vultures”.
This scandal exposes a very serious problem, that our economy is vulnerable to private equity vultures who swoop in and prey on our high street brands by loading them with debt and then trying to ditch them for a profit.
It is deeply concerning to see the uncertainty about Poundland’s future. That’s why I, the Secretary of State and the Prime Minister, have been keeping a close eye on what is an extremely worrying situation for the staff, their families and communities up and down the country. We’ve been demanding to know what is happening, particularly for Gordon Brothers to explain why they haven’t accepted any offer to keep the company going. We continue to establish the facts.
Poundland owner Gordon Brothers accused of 'predatory capitalism'
Poundland’s owner Gordon Brothers has been accused of “predatory capitalism” as 12,000 jobs are under threat, while the government insisted it was working hard to protect “as many jobs as possible,”
Poundland’s future hangs in the balance after the retailer, which is controlled by the US restructuring specialist Gordon Brothers, filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators at the high court last week, with the advisory firm AlixPartners lined up to run the process.
The founder of Poundland, Steve Smith, has warned that staff at the retailer could be out of work for “years” if it collapses, as he called on the owners of the troubled chain to accept a proposed buyout deal.
In response to an urgent question in the House of Commons about the fate of the budget retailer, Kate Dearden, minister in the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade, said officials had met with Gordon Brothers and Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, is due to meet the company “ to continue to press our concerns and establish the facts”.
She said:
We are establishing the facts, keeping in close contact with those involved and monitoring developments closely. The Secretary of State and I continue to engage closely on this issue. We have met and are in going contact with the trade union Usdaw, who I know are extremely concerned about their members’ jobs and their livelihoods, and I want to thank them for their work and engagement. We’re also meeting with Bill Williams, the managing director of Poundland, this week. Earlier this week, officials met with Gordon Brothers and the Secretary of State is due to meet with them.
However, there are ongoing commercial negotiations concerning a private business and it would not be appropriate for government to seek to influence the outcome or comments on the merits of individual bids. The owners should be acting in the best interests of their loyal UK staff and stores. What we want is the best possible outcome for Poundland workforce and the future of the business. The 12,000 staff and the many thousands of suppliers are at the forefront of our minds and we want to see an outcome that protects as many jobs as possible and keeps as much of the business trading as possible.
Gareth Snell, Labour MP for Stoke on Trent Central, then asked:
What can this house do to send a message to Gordon Brothers that the predatory capitalism that they are putting into this company will not be tolerated, because we in this country will always stand with people before profit.
UK’s top polluter Drax could power country’s largest AI datacentre
Jillian Ambrose
Britain’s most polluting power plant could soon power the country’s largest datacentre under a £20bn deal to build AI infrastructure on the site of the Drax power plant in North Yorkshire.
The power plant’s FTSE 250 owner has struck a deal with infrastructure investor Brookfield and and the AI infrastructure platform Radiant to develop a datacentre with an eventual capacity of more than 1 gigawatt which could begin operations by early 2028.
In the initial phase of the project Drax will provide the datacentre project with land and access to the national power grid through existing connections on the site, but it hopes to begin powering the data centre directly by the early 2030s.
Drax said the development could attract more than £20bn ($26.8bn) in investment and represent “the next chapter” for the former power plant after ministers signalled plans to limit its power generation in the future.
Will Gardiner, the chief executive of Drax, said the project would “help secure the long-term future of the site and protect hundreds of jobs” while “supporting the North’s reindustrialisation and strengthening sovereign AI capability”.
The largest power plant in the UK produces almost 5% of the country’s electricity by burning woody biomass pellets, making the site the single largest emitter of carbon dioxide, according to analysts.
These emissions are not accounted for by the UK government because Drax claims that the equivalent carbon emissions are absorbed by growing trees which provide the waste wood used to make the biomass pellets.
Love it or hate it, the 2026 John Lewis Christmas advert is here – and it’s Kristin Scott Thomas v Pickles the evil AI overlord puppy!
The John Lewis Christmas advert no longer lands with the same thud as old. Once it prompted full media saturation and performative crying contests on social media. Now, more often than not, it’s the thing you skip before watching cat videos on YouTube. Nevertheless, its release is still an event, and so here we are again, writes the Guardian’s Stuart Heritage.
This year, either by fluke or by design, John Lewis has managed to remember that it is a shop, and not simply a vessel for feelings of unfathomable sadness. Rather than being a vignette about lonely penguins or Moon Hitlers or Elton John’s growing fears about his own mortality, the John Lewis Christmas advert is literally about a woman going shopping. Admittedly there are caveats, but we’ll get to those. For the most part, this is less ‘Christmas can be emotionally brutal’ and more ‘Hey guys, remember shops?’ That has to be a good thing.
Garry White, chief investment commentator at the US investment bank Raymond James, said that Primark will need a disciplined returns policy for its planned new home delivery service.
Home delivery is an obvious gap in Primark’s proposition, but it will need to be managed carefully given the retailer’s position at the value end of the market.
The experience of other online fashion retailers shows that shoppers often order multiple sizes or styles with the intention of returning unwanted items, resulting in far higher return rates than those seen in physical stores.
Returns can be expensive, generating costs related to shipping, handling, quality checks, repackaging and, in some cases, markdowns on items that can no longer be sold at full price. As a result, Primark will need a disciplined returns policy if it is to keep costs under control and protect margins.
The struggling British supermarket chain Asda has appointed the 69-year-old former Morrisons boss, David Potts, as chief executive with immediate effect.
Allan Leighton, 73, who has served as Asda’s executive chairman since November 2024, will take a step back and become non-executive chair “as planned,” Asda said.
Leighton said:
I am really excited to have appointed David as Group CEO. Over the last two years, we have stabilised the business and returned it to some growth and begun to establish Asda as ‘more than a supermarket’ through our Formula for Growth strategy.
David has an outstanding record in our industry, his experience is exactly what we now require for the next stage of our transformation and beyond and it will be great to work with him.
And Potts said:
Asda has long been a great business, one I’ve admired and traded against over many years. The colleagues are remarkable, some of the most passionate I’ve met.
The business has made good progress but significant opportunities remain and I’m delighted and very proud to have been asked by Allan to lead the team.
Providing value to families across the UK has always been in Asda’s DNA and by making improvements to the shopping trip every week, which customers can experience and feel in their pockets, we will revitalise the business and bring benefits for all our stakeholders, including our 116,296 very hard-working colleagues.
Christmas is upon us and the business has a clear focus on keeping Asda prices locked low at this important time for our customers. I’m excited to get started.
In August, Asda heralded its first trading growth in more than two years, with Leighton saying that it was attracting more shoppers with lower prices and an improved online service.
However, Aldi is poised to overtake Asda to become the UK’s third-largest supermarket, with less than 1 percentage point separating them.
They may be two of the most recognisable brands in Britain, with a combined 188 years serving shoppers, but industry watchers agree that either Asda or Morrisons – or both – could disappear within a decade.
Primark to launch home delivery in Great Britain before end of 2027
Exciting news for Primark shoppers: it will launch a home delivery service in Great Britain before the end of next year.
George Weston, the chief executive of the clothing chain’s parent company Associated British Foods, told Reuters:
Home delivery, we’ll launch by the end of 2027.
We’re sure it will be incremental [for sales] and profitable.
ABF intends to spin off Primark in December 2027, separating it from its sugar business.
In September, ABF said Primark would launch home delivery “in the future”.
Until now, the company – which already offers a click and collect service – has shied away from home delivery, arguing that its low prices made it too difficult to absorb the cost of packing and shipping orders.
Stock markets slide as oil prices rebound after new US strikes on Iran
Stock markets have fallen in early trading, as new strikes by the US on Iran led to a rebound in crude oil prices, dampening hopes for new peace talks to bring the eight-month war to an end.
The UK’s FTSE 100 index is down nearly 44 points at 10,717, a 0.4% drop. Germany’s Dax slid 1%, France’s CAC 40 is down 0.6%, and Italy’s FTSE MiB and Spain’s Ibex both lost around 0.9%.
Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, is trading 1.7% higher at $106.55, a day after it fell sharply towards $103 a barrel. The US carried out strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island in the strait of Hormuz, a US official said – a day after Iran signalled it was open to peace talks and Donald Trump also suggested he would give diplomacy a chance until after the US midterm elections.
The strikes also came hours after the US vice-president, JD Vance, said he was optimistic that diplomatic efforts to end the war were moving in the right direction.
Primark owner Associated British Foods is is among the main FTSE 100 losers, after it forecast another year of falling profits because of deeper losses in its sugar business and weaker sales at Primark. Mining shares Anglo American, Antofagasta, Fresnillo and Endeavour Mining and commodities trader Glencore are leading the blue-chip index lower.
Hugo Boss shares fell 2.6% in early trading in Frankfurt after the German fashion retailer cut its sales and profit outlook as it pointed to weak consumer demand.
Bucking the trend, shares in the German pharmaceuticals and crop science company Bayer jumped 5.6% after it lifted its 2026 profit outlook.
Virgin Media O2 to cut thousands of jobs as it plans £800m cost savings
Mark Sweney
Virgin Media O2 is to cut thousands of UK jobs in an £800m cost-cutting drive as the telecommunications company aims to tackle its £22bn debt pile.
VMO2, which is jointly owned by the British-Dutch-American telecoms company Liberty Global and Spain’s Telefónica, said £300m of the savings target will come from job cuts that will reduce the company’s employee wage bill by 30% over the next two years.
The company did not specify how many jobs this will equate to, but it could be as many as 25% of its 16,000 workforce.
The company, which said that most of the job losses will come from non-customer facing roles, said it intends to increase the use of AI tools in areas including customer service, network planning and fault management.
The VMO2 chief executive, Lutz Schüler, said:
While we will give a fuller update on the new strategic plan in the coming months, we are already progressing and making difficult decisions to prioritise investments and reduce costs which includes the size of our workforce.
Standing still and doing what we’ve always done is not an option and while many of these decisions are tough, they are necessary for our future success and growth. Virgin Media O2 must evolve, and the action needed to make that happen starts now.
However on Monday, the global oil benchmark plunged 11% to $103.28 a barrel after Donald Trump reportedly said he was willing to give diplomacy more time.
Amin H. Nasser, Aramco’s president and chief executive, said:
Geopolitical uncertainty and attacks on key energy facilities continued to amplify the global energy supply crisis in the third quarter of 2026, with serious implications for global energy security. Despite challenges, the unwavering dedication of our workforce, our operational excellence, the flexibility of our system, and the strength of a supply network built over decades enabled us to continue delivering reliably to our customers through this extraordinary period.
We continue to explore additional overseas storage capacity and alternative export routes to further strengthen our global supply network, and our robust operational and financial performance during this volatile period demonstrates the value of our resilience.
This means that the world’s biggest oil companies are on track for combined profits of around $100bn between July and September.
Australia’s central bank has lifted interest rates for the fifth time this year, taking them to the highest level in 18 years.
The Reserve Bank of Australia’s board raised its cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.85% and said it will continue to do what it considers necessary to bring inflation to target. However, it dropped its previous guidance that it would raise the cash rate further if needed.
And a surprisingly narrow 6-3 vote indicated policymakers may be getting to the end of their rate hikes.
Michele Bullock, the governor, said it was “not the news that many Australians want to hear”, but it would prevent “even worse pain down the track”.
She said it was unclear what the next move in rates will be, adding that the three dissenting members stressed downside risks such as the weakening housing market and rising unemployment.
After five rate hikes this year, she said it is an appropriate time to pause and assess how the economy is responding to the rate rises, but cautioned that
there is still a bit of a skew on the upside to inflation risks, and we need to be alert to those materialising.
Updated forecasts from the central bank show headline inflation hitting 4.5% in the fourth quarter, before easing back to the target range of 2% to 3% in the second half of next year. Unemployment is forecast to rise above 5% in the next couple of years.
Ipek Ozkardeskaya, senior analyst at Swissquote, said:
Higher energy prices… would strengthen the case for further monetary policy tightening by the Federal Reserve (Fed) and other major central banks. The Reserve Bank of Australia delivered a 25bp hike today, as expected, while the Bank of England (BoE) is widely expected to announce a 25bp hike on Thursday, following a rather uneventful budget announcement last week that allows the BoE to go on with its life — and take care of its inflation problem.
The Big Picture
Overall, if we take a step back and look at the bigger picture, the latest monetary policy decisions have brought either rate hikes or the prospect of tighter monetary policy to fight inflation fuelled by elevated global energy prices. On top of that, many developed-market bond yields face upward pressure from intensifying fiscal concerns, while large bond issuance by technology companies to finance their massive AI buildout could add to that pressure.
The cryptocurrency exchange Binance said hourly deposits exceeded withdrawals this morning, suggesting flows are stabilising after its hack last week. This resulted in $6.3bn of assets being stolen from customer accounts.

items.title: Asda hires supermarket boss who sold Morrisons to private equity
items.summary: After a long search for a new chief executive, Britain's third largest grocer said that David Potts has joined the ailing firm with immediate effect.
items.body:
Asda hires supermarket boss who sold Morrisons to private equity
Asda has brought in the former boss of Morrisons who oversaw the sale of the rival supermarket to private equity.
After a long search for a new chief executive, Britain’s third-largest grocer said that David Potts had joined the ailing firm with immediate effect.
For the past two years, the business has been run by retail veteran and former Asda boss Allan Leighton, who will now move into a non-executive chairman role.
But analysts were split on whether the appointment would 'move the needle' for Asda, which has battled falling sales since private equity firm TDR Capital helped to finance a debt-fuelled £6.8billion takeover by the billionaire Issa brothers in 2021.
The supermarket has since lost out to discounters Lidl and Aldi, and grappled with debt pressures and severe disruption linked to an IT upgrade.
Leighton said the group had ‘stabilised’ under his leadership - after last month reporting quarterly sales growth for the first time in more than two years.
New Asda boss David Potts said that the supermarket has made 'good progress but significant opportunities remain'.
And he said that Potts’ experience was ‘exactly what we now require for the next stage of our transformation’.
Potts, who began his career at Tesco, said: 'Asda has long been a great business, one I’ve admired and traded against over many years.
‘The business has made good progress but significant opportunities remain and I’m delighted and very proud to have been asked by Allan to lead the team.’
Potts began his career at Tesco on the shop floor aged 16 and, after failing his O-Levels, worked his way up to run its Ireland business, its UK business and its Asia business. He was also on the board of the supermarket giant from 1998 to 2012.
He led Morrisons from 2015 to 2023, a period which included the group’s £10billion sale to private equity group Clayton Dubilier & Rice in 2021. Morrisons has also struggled in the wake of its debt-fuelled takeover and even lost its spot as Britain’s fifth biggest grocer to discounter Lidl.
Potts ‘faces one of the toughest turnaround jobs in modern British retail at Asda, but his track record at Morrisons doesn't necessarily inspire absolute confidence,’ according to Jonathan de Mello, founder and CEO at retail consultancy JDM Retail.
He said that both supermarkets ‘have perennially suffered from a lack of a truly distinctive offer and an inability to undercut the discounters on price, leaving them as the primary losers in the ongoing supermarket price wars.’
He added: ‘Unless [Potts] can aggressively invest in a distinctive, value-driven strategy rather than relying on defensive cost-cutting, it is difficult to see how his appointment moves the needle for a business that remains deeply exposed in a hyper-competitive market.’
Clive Black, the influential retail analyst at Shore Capital, disagreed calling it a 'very strongly positive appointment'.
'David Potts is one of the greatest grocers ever to walk the aisles of Britain,' he said. 'We expect Mr Potts, who is very experienced, fit as a flea, but also tactically savvy, to bring a fresh pair of eyes to Asda.
'It will not be, to us, Morrisonification or Tescofication of his new home. We do, however, anticipate that bit by bit he will smarten up and sharpen up the business.'
Earlier this year, Leighton said that Asda was 'about a third' of the way through its recovery, which has seen the supermarket slash prices and upgrade its online operations.
Leighton, who rejoined the Leeds-based retailer in November 2024, has warned that his revival plan will not be an overnight fix and slashing prices will hit profits.
But he said there was pressure on prices due to the heatwave affecting crops this summer.
Asda accounts revealed that pre-tax losses had widened from £599million in 2024 to £989million in 2025, as total sales fell 3.4 per cent to £25.9billion.

items.title: Primark confirms plans to launch home delivery - but not until the end of 2027
items.summary: Primark confirmed it will launch home delivery at the end of next year in a bid to reassure potential investors over the spin-off from its owner.
items.body:
Primark confirms plans to launch home delivery - but not until the end of 2027
Primark confirmed it will launch home delivery at the end of next year in a bid to reassure potential investors over the spin-off from its owner.
The clothing retailer plans to launch online orders before the end of next year to coincide with the demerger from its owner, Associated British Foods.
The group has moved closer to online retail in recent years, launching a mobile app for British customers earlier this year to support its overdue move into click-and-collect, which debuted in November 2022.
Primark previously argued as recently as May that its low prices and tight margins cannot absorb the additional costs related to online delivery, before announcing plans to introduce the service in Great Britain.
George Weston, the boss of parent Associated British Foods, said: ‘Neither [the demerger and launching deliveries] is dependent on the other, of course.
'But having home delivery on the horizon, I hope will reassure potential investors in Primark that we're creating an omnichannel retailer which is super relevant to all the shoppers in its markets.’
Bosses believe the parts of ABF will do better as stand-alone companies than as a combined conglomerate.
Bosses say Primark is recovering after battling a tough consumer environment
But experts have warned that the business needs to show signs of recovering sales at Primark while its loss-making sugar arm also weighs on buzz around a demerger.
Primark’s like-for-like sales fell 2.6 per cent due to a ‘challenging consumer environment across most markets’, the retailer said.
But Weston said there were ‘so many positive things to point to’ and that Primark was ‘well on its way back ', pointing to sales growth in the UK in recent weeks.
He said offering customers affordable prices at Christmas was essential, including £1.30 Christmas T-shirts for children.
Ranges including family pyjama sets and a ‘festive glamour’ collection by Coleen Rooney are also expected to do well.
The brand is due to split from ABF's food businesses by December 2027. Should Primark list in London, it would also boost the beleaguered stock market as its size means it is set to sail straight into the FTSE-100.
Analysts are unconvinced splitting Primark will deliver
'The uncomfortable truth is that the real opportunity to spin off Primark at a premium valuation was the best part of two decades ago,' said Chris Beckett, analyst at Quilter Cheviot. 'Primark is still a strong retailer, but today it is a more mature business facing margin pressure, so it is difficult to see the demerger unlocking a significant amount of value on its own.'
Mark Crouch, analyst at eToro said: 'The planned separation of Primark from ABF's food businesses could give investors a clearer picture of what each is worth. But splitting the group will not solve its underlying problems.
'Management must demonstrate that home delivery can deliver profitable growth, while ensuring both businesses emerge from the separation with stronger prospects than they have today."
ABF said profits are set to fall again next year after a ‘challenging’ environment over the past year.
Profits plummeted 14 per cent to £1.46 billion for the year to September 12, compared with the previous year.
Shares in ABF fell 3.3 per cent to 1,878p, bringing the year's losses to 11 per cent.

UK food suppliers hit by European cyberattacks
items.summary: British food suppliers have been caught up in a wave of cyberattacks targeting supermarket refrigerators across Europe, prompting warnings that outdated technology is leaving the UK’s food supply chain exposed. The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) confirmed on Tuesday that vulnerable refrigeration technology had been exploited in a small number of incidents in Britain, after [...]
items.body:
UK food suppliers hit by European cyberattacks
British food suppliers have been caught up in a wave of cyberattacks targeting supermarket refrigerators across Europe, prompting warnings that outdated technology is leaving the UK’s food supply chain exposed.
The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) confirmed on Tuesday that vulnerable refrigeration technology had been exploited in a small number of incidents in Britain, after hackers remotely manipulated supermarket fridge temperatures across several European countries.
The attacks have forced retailers in Sweden, Belgium, Ireland and elsewhere to throw away large quantities of fresh and frozen food after refrigeration systems were switched into defrost mode.
Richard Horne, chief executive of the NCSC, said the agency had “worked through the night” to warn potentially affected British businesses.
The British Association of Independent Meat Suppliers, which represents more than 300 businesses, confirmed that some members had been affected, although none had lost any inventory.
The incidents follow a similar attack on hundreds of French supermarkets last month, which caused millions of euros in damage after hackers exploited vulnerabilities in remotely managed fridges.
Hundreds of UK systems exposed
Cyber security researchers have identified more than 800 fridge interfaces associated with British retailers that are accessible over the public internet.
While that does not necessarily mean the systems can be hacked, experts warn that outdated software and poorly secured remote access can leave critical equipment vulnerable.
Martin Riley, chief technology officer at cyber security firm Bridewell, said the food industry was particularly exposed because its products were perishable and operations depended on tightly controlled temperatures.
“A supermarket fridge holds no secrets. It holds a temperature. Change that temperature overnight and you destroy the value of everything inside it within hours,” he said. “There is no backup to restore from. The stock is simply gone.”
Riley said his firm’s research had identified more than 6,000 refrigeration management panels from a single manufacturer exposed online worldwide.
He warned that attackers were increasingly targeting operational technology, the systems controlling physical equipment, rather than simply stealing data or locking businesses out of their IT networks.
Fears over food security
The incidents have raised concerns about the wider consequences of cyberattacks on essential infrastructure, particularly as supermarkets increasingly rely on internet-connected equipment and third-party contractors.
“The cyberattacks affecting supermarkets across the UK and Europe show how incidents can quickly extend beyond IT disruption, affecting food supplies, businesses and consumers,” said Charl van der Walt, global head of security research at Orange Cyberdefense.
“As in the French refrigerator case, the perpetrators and their motives remain unclear, as does whether the incidents are connected”.
He added that attacks did not need to be deliberately designed to spread fear to have that effect.
“When attackers remain hidden, technical details are difficult to verify and the public is left uncertain, trust can quickly erode.”
Ed Hayes, data protection partner at law firm TLT, said operational technology had historically been a “cybersecurity blind-spot”, with retailers investing more heavily in protecting payment systems and customer data than refrigeration and logistics equipment.
“Legacy OT systems that were never designed with cyber resilience in mind are frequently still in use, running without basic security controls,” he said.
The latest incidents come after cyberattacks on Marks & Spencer and the Co-op last year disrupted deliveries and left supermarket shelves empty.
The British Retail Consortium said retailers were working with the NCSC to strengthen their defences against similar attacks.
The NCSC has not identified who is responsible for the latest incidents, with Horne saying it remains “too early to say” who was behind them.

items.title: Christmas campaigns 2026: Shoppers want lower prices, so why are retailers betting big on festive storytelling?
items.summary: From John Lewis’s talking toy dog to Asda’s festive rave, retailers are taking very different approaches to Christmas 2026. Early audience research suggests shoppers enjoy the spectacle, even as they question whether brands should be spending so much on it… Kevin the Carrot is busy looking for a missing dog, and it seems that the...
items.body:
From John Lewis’s talking toy dog to Asda’s festive rave, retailers are taking very different approaches to Christmas 2026. Early audience research suggests shoppers enjoy the spectacle, even as they question whether brands should be spending so much on it…
Kevin the Carrot is busy looking for a missing dog, and it seems that the BFG is feeling poorly. Richard Ayoade is being visited by Argos toys, while Dame Kristin Scott Thomas is taking present-buying advice from a talking wooden dog.
At Asda, meanwhile, Christmas has become a rave.
Britain’s retailers are back in their festive advertising finery. But while agencies debate who has made the season’s most moving film, shoppers have a less romantic suggestion; make Christmas cheaper.
In research carried out by OnePulse before this year’s supermarket campaigns launched, 57 per cent of UK consumers said they would rather retailers spent less on Christmas advertising and passed the savings on through lower prices. And 61 per cent said a Christmas advert had never changed where they did their main festive food shop.
Yet show people the adverts, and the response is rather warmer. In OnePulse’s early testing, Sainsbury’s and John Lewis both averaged 3.8 out of five, while Tesco scored 3.6. Some 72 per cent liked or loved Sainsbury’s BFG campaign; 68 per cent felt the same about John Lewis.
So, shoppers can resent the spend and enjoy the result. Yet for those on the coalface of these marketing efforts, it raises a more useful question than which film wins Christmas. What does that enjoyment actually do for the business?
The price of Christmas magic
This is hardly an easy year in which to defend a lavish production budget. Sensormatic Solutions found that 63 per cent of consumers prioritise price when gift shopping, while the average planned Christmas budget has fallen 10 per cent year on year to £504.70.
Asda has responded with its high-energy ‘All of Christmas at Asda Price. BOOM!’ campaign, trading the traditional tearjerker for dancing, noise and a very obvious value message.
“The reality is customers don’t want to do less at Christmas, they simply want to spend less on it,” says Asda group marketing director Tom Hampson.
It’s a clear proposition. But wanting low prices at the checkout isn’t the same as wanting to watch an advert about them. OnePulse found that 42 per cent of shoppers wanted joyful, uplifting fun from festive supermarket advertising, while 28 per cent wanted warmth and comfort.
And that leaves room for something less transactional.
Comfort sells…but does nostalgia?
Sainsbury’s has returned to Roald Dahl’s BFG for a third Christmas. In The Big Delivery, the giant has fallen ill and supermarket colleague Annie brings him a festive feast. There’s plenty of familiar fantasy, but also a starring role for the retailer’s Taste the Difference food.
The formula appears to be landing. Some 51 per cent of respondents in OnePulse’s launch-period testing said the advert made them feel festive, and 63 per cent wanted the BFG back next year.
Melissa Minkow, global director, retail strategy and insights at CI&T, thinks comfort has a particular appeal in an exhausting news environment.
“Given the intensity of the 24/7 news cycle and the chaos that comes with that, I would think consumers will be broadly appreciative of any marketing efforts that provide feelings of comfort,” she says.
“Comfort is an easily uniting, safe sentiment, so brands would be wise to create content that delivers on that emotion.”
Minkow particularly enjoyed Sainsbury’s Roald Dahl campaign. She also points to Gen Z’s appetite for 1990s fashion and music as a reminder that nostalgia needn’t depend on remembering an era first-hand.
Aldi clearly sees value in familiarity, too. Its latest teaser brings back Kevin the Carrot (a now ten-year-old mascot for the festive season), searching for Cauli Dog. OnePulse found that 63 per cent of shoppers wanted Kevin to return.
Very’s flamingo family tells a similar story about the rewards of consistency. The company says recognition of its brand campaigns has doubled since the characters arrived in 2023. Its new, AI-assisted advert earned a 5.9-star System1 score, the strongest pre-launch result Very has recorded.
Those measures aren’t directly comparable with OnePulse’s enjoyment ratings. But they highlight an important fact. A familiar character can entertain today and, over time, make a brand easier to recognise tomorrow.
The celebrity alternative
Other retailers are pursuing attention through star power. Sports Direct and Nike have recruited Erling Haaland and a cast of sporting and music stars, while Argos has cast Richard Ayoade in a Christmas Carol-inspired journey through the retailer’s past.
And Tesco’s The Wrong Address stars Roisin Conaty and Anna Maxwell Martin as old friends reunited by a grocery delivery mix-up. The film made 28 per cent of OnePulse viewers well up.
Interestingly, just 17 per cent of consumers in OnePulse’s earlier survey said they preferred celebrities in supermarket Christmas ads. After seeing Tesco’s film, however, 71 per cent of respondents thought its casting was the right choice.
People aren’t necessarily good at predicting the creative work they will like. As Minkow observes, familiar nostalgia and contemporary celebrity can both cut through when used well. The question is whether people remember the retailer as clearly as the famous face.
From affection to action
John Lewis has arguably made that question the subject of its own advert. In Gloria and Pickles, Kristin Scott Thomas plays a grandmother on the verge of putting cash in envelopes until a toy dog nudges her towards more thoughtful presents.
The commercial ambition is hardly hidden: ‘Don’t give up on giving’ is a plea to buy a gift rather than hand over money. John Lewis marketing and loyalty director Rosie Hanley has admitted the dilemma is familiar: “I’ve definitely resorted to putting cash in an envelope for fear of getting it wrong.”
Among OnePulse viewers, 36 per cent said the advert made them more likely to shop at John Lewis. But 48 per cent picked the dog as the standout feature, while only 12 per cent spontaneously mentioned its thoughtful-gifting message.
That’s not a failure. People rarely recite brand strategies when asked what they liked about an advert. It does, though, expose the difficulty of turning a memorable film into a memorable reason to shop.
The same conundrum runs through the numbers elsewhere. Despite Sainsbury’s strong enjoyment score, 56 per cent of its viewers said they would rather the money had gone towards lower prices. And reported purchase intention is not the same thing as an actual sale.
The real test will, of course, arrive after the heartwarming stories and celebrity appearances have faded. Did the work improve brand preference, bring customers into shops and online, and create value that lasts beyond December? Only time will tell.
There may be no single winning creative formula this Christmas. Asda wants to own value; Sainsbury’s wants its premium food associated with celebration; Argos wants shoppers to reconsider its range; John Lewis wants them to buy thoughtful gifts.
And, it’s perfectly possible to love an advert about a poorly giant and still wish the Christmas dinner in your basket cost less.

items.title: Asda appoints former Morrisons boss David Potts as group CEO
items.summary: Asda has appointed former Morrisons chief executive David Potts CBE as its new group CEO with immediate effect, it has been revealed. Potts takes the helm as Allan Leighton moves into the role of non-executive group chairman, as previously planned, where he will focus on the retailer’s long-term strategic direction. Asda is looking to build...
items.body:
Asda has appointed former Morrisons chief executive David Potts CBE as its new group CEO with immediate effect, it has been revealed.
Potts takes the helm as Allan Leighton moves into the role of non-executive group chairman, as previously planned, where he will focus on the retailer’s long-term strategic direction.
Asda is looking to build on its Formula for Growth strategy, which Leighton said had helped stabilise the business, return it to growth and establish its position as “more than a supermarket”.
Leighton said: “I am really excited to have appointed David as Group CEO.
“Over the last two years, we have stabilised the business and returned it to some growth and begun to establish Asda as ‘more than a supermarket’ through our Formula for Growth strategy.
“David has an outstanding record in our industry, his experience is exactly what we now require for the next stage of our transformation and beyond and it will be great to work with him.”
Potts brings decades of grocery retail experience, having started his career on the Tesco shop floor aged 16 before rising through the ranks to lead its UK, Ireland and Asia operations.
He went on to become chief executive of Morrisons in 2015, where he oversaw a turnaround of the business, expanded its wholesale and convenience operations and guided its transition to private ownership before departing in 2023.
Speaking about his appointment, Potts said: “Asda has long been a great business, one I’ve admired and traded against over many years. The colleagues are remarkable, some of the most passionate I’ve met.
“The business has made good progress but significant opportunities remain and I’m delighted and very proud to have been asked by Allan to lead the team.”
Potts said improving the customer shopping experience and delivering value would be central to his plans to revitalise the supermarket chain.
“Providing value to families across the UK has always been in Asda’s DNA and by making improvements to the shopping trip every week, which customers can experience and feel in their pockets, we will revitalise the business and bring benefits for all our stakeholders, including our 116,296 very hard-working colleagues.”
He added that Asda’s immediate priority would be keeping prices low during the crucial Christmas trading period.
“Christmas is upon us and the business has a clear focus on keeping Asda prices locked low at this important time for our customers. I’m excited to get started.”

items.title: Virgin Media O2 to cut thousands of jobs as it plans £800m cost savings
items.summary: Up to 25% of 16,000 workforce could go as telecoms group says it will increase use of AI in areas including customer service Business live – latest updates Virgin Media O2 is to cut thousands of jobs in an £800m cost-cutting drive as the telecommunications company aims to tackle its £22bn debt pile. VMO2, which is jointly owned by Liberty Global and Telefónica, said £300m of the savings target will come from job cuts that will reduce the company’s employee wage bill by 30% over the next two years. Continue reading...
items.body:
Virgin Media O2 is to cut thousands of jobs in an £800m cost-cutting drive as the telecommunications company aims to tackle its £22bn debt pile.
VMO2, which is jointly owned by Liberty Global and Telefónica, said £300m of the savings target will come from job cuts that will reduce the company’s employee wage bill by 30% over the next two years.
The company did not specify how many jobs this will equate to, but it could be as many as 25% of its 16,000 workforce.
“While we will give a fuller update on the new strategic plan in the coming months, we are already progressing and making difficult decisions to prioritise investments and reduce costs which includes the size of our workforce,” said the VMO2 chief executive, Lutz Schüler.
“Standing still and doing what we’ve always done is not an option and while many of these decisions are tough, they are necessary for our future success and growth. Virgin Media O2 must evolve, and the action needed to make that happen starts now.”
The company, which said that most of the job losses will come from non-customer facing roles, said it intends to increase the use of AI tools in areas including customer service, network planning and fault management. It has offices in London, Reading and Dublin.
The cost-cutting plans, which will save £800m annually by 2029, also include making savings by reducing the use of contractors and reviewing suppliers and supply chain contracts.
Noel McClean, the deputy general of the Prospect union, said that the scale of the cuts will be “devastating” for staff and significantly impact the operation of the business.
“The proposed 30% reduction in the VMO2 workforce [costs] will be devastating for those directly affected and will of course have an impact on colleagues remaining in the business,” he said.
“Industry conditions are tough but this level of cuts will drastically alter the way VMO2 works. As a union we have vast experience of this kind of restructure and stand ready to work with the employer.”
The Communication Workers Union (CWU) said it hoped the large-scale job cuts could be managed on a voluntary basis to minimise the impact on staff.
“The most recent news, briefed out to the media, will undoubtedly leave members feeling stressed and worried about their long-term job prospects,” Stephen Albon, an assistant secretary at the CWU, said. “The CWU wishes to work with the company to mitigate these losses and will be urging the company to explore a voluntary approach to them.”
VMO2 has also moved to reduce capital expenditure by halting investment in upgrading its network to full fibre, which is 50% complete, beyond existing commitments it has with partners.
Instead the company will make a low-cost upgrade that will lead to most of the network that has not transitioned to full fibre being improved to 2Gbps speeds by the end of next year.
VMO2 said it is exploring wholesale deals to expand its services in areas its network does not cover, confirming reports that it is close to a deal with BT’s Openreach to extend its footprint from 19m to potentially 25m homes.
The company also looks poised to slash its dividend, saying it is “reviewing options” relating to cash distributions to shareholders this year.
The business said it expects to incur £250m in restructuring costs.
The cuts were announced alongside VMO2’s latest results, which showed the company shed 23,300 broadband and 7,800 consumer mobile customers, in the quarter to the end of September.
“The direction we’re setting today paves the way for the next chapter of Virgin Media O2: a company that will be leaner, clearer on priorities and faster in delivery,” Schuler said.
The cuts were announced alongside VMO2’s latest results, which showed the company shed 23,300 broadband and 7,800 consumer mobile customers in the quarter to the end of September.
Earlier this month, VMO2 lashed out at a decision to fast-track BT’s £400m rescue of TalkTalk, while at the same time the UK competition regulator has signalled that it might block the £2bn takeover of Netomnia by Nexfibre, whose investors include Liberty Global and Telefonica.
The Competition and Markets Authority said that its preference is for Netomnia to be bought by CityFibre – to create a stronger third challenger to Openreach – but it has a significant debt pile and is in restructure talks with lenders.

items.body:
This November, Froot Pops, the UK’s leading frozen fruit snacking brand, is expanding its product portfolio with the launch of Sours. The new range of confectionery inspired frozen fruit snacks will be rolling out with Ocado from 4th November. Launching in two flavours, Zingy Blueberry and Hot Mango (RRP:£6 / 220g bag), Sours marks the brand’s latest move to broaden its offering beyond chocolate-coated frozen fruit and bring new flavour experiences to the freezer aisle. Both SKUs will also be available to independent retailers via wholesalers including CLF, OnTheRocks, Nice London and Woodford Dairies.
Drawing inspiration from the bold, punchy flavours traditionally associated with confectionery, Froot Pops Sours combine real frozen fruit with zingy, flavour-packed coatings, delivering a playful new twist on frozen snacking. Made with no artificial colours, flavours or preservatives, the range offers consumers an exciting alternative to traditional frozen treats.
Making its market debut with Ocado, Hot Mango Sours combines the tropical sweetness of real mango with a tangy sour chilli coating, delivering a distinctive combination of sweet, sour and heat. Zingy Blueberry features whole blueberries, picked at peak freshness and sourced from trusted farms, coated in a naturally zingy blend of sour lemon and dragon fruit.
The launch follows an encouraging start for Blueberry Sours which launched into Tesco Ireland in September, where the product achieved one of the highest rates of sale in the frozen category and exceeded initial demand expectations. The range extension aims to answer growing consumer appetite for sour flavour profiles, with sour-flavoured fruit sweets reportedly growing 4.5 times faster than the total sweets market, now accounting for 12% of the market and £171m in sales.
Froot Pops founder Ana Martins said: “We see a huge opportunity to bring the bold, exciting flavour experiences traditionally associated with confectionery into frozen snacking. With Sours, we’re taking everything consumers love about sweet-and-sour treats and giving it a fresh, fruity twist. While we’ve built our reputation on chocolate-coated frozen fruit, our ambition has always been bigger than that. We want to demonstrate just how much potential there is for innovation within frozen snacking, introducing new flavours, textures and experiences that give consumers more reasons to reach for the freezer and retailers more opportunities to engage shoppers.
The response to Blueberry Sours in Tesco Ireland has been incredibly encouraging, with the product selling out in just three days. It’s a strong indication of the appetite for more adventurous flavours in frozen and gives us a fantastic foundation for introducing the range to UK shoppers, alongside our brand-new Hot Mango Sours.”
The launch comes as consumer interest in frozen continues to grow. Ocado Retail recently reported an 18% year-on-year increase in frozen product sales, with frozen fruit sales rising 23% over the same period. Meanwhile, 47% of UK adults say they have increased their frozen purchases in the past year. Froot Pops is looking to build on this momentum, extending its proposition beyond chocolate-coated fruit and reinforcing its ambition to make frozen snacking a more exciting and relevant choice for everyday occasions.

items.summary: Morrisons has partnered with Duvo.ai as it looks to identify opportunities to make greater use of AI across its existing systems.Duvo was co-founded by Tomáš Čupr, who founded Rohlik Group, the European online grocer. It identifies and automates repetitive business tasks, freeing up team members to
items.body:
Morrisons has partnered with Duvo.ai as it looks to identify opportunities to make greater use of AI across its existing systems.
Duvo was co-founded by Tomáš Čupr, who founded Rohlik Group, the European online grocer. It identifies and automates repetitive business tasks, freeing up team members to focus on decision-making, creativity, customer service and partner relationships.
The project will start by capturing how processes actually work across the UK grocery retailer's people, teams and systems. Duvo will then help it identify opportunities to simplify and redesign those processes, focusing where AI can create the most value, and highlighting a pathway for their swift adoption into everyday operations.
"Our business processes have evolved over decades and Duvo gives us a way to understand them in detail, and quickly," says Gordon MacPherson, Group Productivity Director at Morrisons, which recently brought in Dr Mohsen Ghasempour as Chief AI Officer.
"It means decisions about which repetitive everyday tasks to simplify, redesign and automate can be based on evidence rather than assumptions. That will give us a much clearer path from identifying AI opportunities to putting them into operation, freeing up our people to concentrate on high value work for the benefit of colleagues and customers."
"The future of AI in retail will be measured by operational outcomes: an invoice matched, a dispute resolved with the evidence attached, or the correct result written back to a core system," says Čupr.
"Getting there starts with understanding how the work actually happens today. Morrisons is doing exactly that. We believe AI should execute work inside the systems teams already use, with the right human oversight and controls, rather than becoming another layer of disconnected pilots. Together, we want to make outcome driven AI part of everyday retail operations at a retailer of this scale.
Duvo’s work in the UK is supported by STROS Partnerships, whose founder, Ross Eggleton, spent much of his career in retail operations, including as Executive Group Director for Logistics, Supply Chain and Technology at Morrisons.
He comments: "Plenty of technology has been sold into retail promising to optimise processes and teams, and most of it has not survived contact with a live operation. Duvo is different, because it learns the real process before it changes anything."

items.title: Why the battle for Poundland is vital for the health of Britain's High Streets: MAGGIE PAGANO
items.summary: What on earth is going on at Poundland? Internal figures trading at the discount retailer is 'flying' but it is on the verge of collapse.
items.body:
Why the battle for Poundland is vital for the health of Britain's High Streets: MAGGIE PAGANO
What on earth is going on at Poundland? Internal figures show that trading at the discount retailer is ‘flying’, that sales are up around 10 per cent, while margins and gross profits are running ahead of expectations.
What’s more extraordinary is that there are two takeover bids on the table – a generous one from the management team and another from the Martin Property Group, a Northern Irish family-run business, which has offered to buy all 600 stores across the country.
Poundland’s founder, Steve Smith, has also made a last-minute intervention, saying he would be interested in joining a takeover bid for the chain to prevent its collapse.
Writing on LinkedIn yesterday, Smith said the group could and should be saved as it had a thriving future, and warned that there will be no High Street revival without Poundland.
Yet, despite these positive signs, Poundland’s private equity owner, Gordon Brothers, is still intent on driving the store chain into the ground, having filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators to Poundland at the High Court.
What is even more tragic is that the reason given by Gordon Brothers is a predictable one: old-fashioned greed.
Poundland's private equity owner Gordon Brothers is intending to break up the High Street chain
Sources close to the US investment firm say it will make more from the break-up of Poundland than from the Martin offer, which is less than the £30million in debt that Gordon Brothers took on when it bought the chain for £1 just over a year ago.
That may be the case. And you could argue that if Gordon Brothers wants to get out – they clearly didn’t do their sums properly – it has every right to do so in the most profitable way it can.
But that would not be the right thing to do. Business owners have broader responsibilities to their employees, and the communities they operate in.
The closure of Poundland would be devastating: 12,000 jobs are at immediate risk and another 18,000 could be lost in the supply chain.
As well as the loss of jobs, Smith is also right when he points out that Poundland is one of the biggest draws on the High Street, and its departure would leave gaping holes in already run-down town centres.
Unusually, though, disaster could be avoided if everybody involved got their act together.
This is why the Government is right to put pressure on Gordon Brothers, with business minister Kate Dearden due to meet Poundland bosses before the Thursday rescue deadline.
Quite what the Government can do, however, is the more pertinent question. There is no obvious pressure or sanction which can be applied, but there is an imperative: if Poundland goes bust, the taxpayer will have to pay millions in welfare benefits to those losing their jobs.
Dearden should make her meeting as public as possible, invite the directors into the House of Commons and make sure the spotlight is on them.
If arm twisting won’t work, maybe Gordon Brothers can be shamed into accepting one of the offers.
Andy Burnham and John Healey want to support our High Streets, they should take a look at the Poundland saga and learn from it
Beware when a brickmaker issues a profit warning
Buckle up your belts. Britain’s biggest brick maker, Ibstock, has issued its second profit warning of the year.
The Leicestershire-based business reports that brick sales have collapsed by more than a fifth so it too has slashed back production by more than a fifth.
Boss Joe Hudson blames some of the downturn on Labour for not getting on with its promised support scheme to help first-time buyers in England buy new homes with a 2.5 per cent deposit.
Labour’s decision to delay the scheme until April will only make the housing market more fragile, particularly with interest rates expected to rise this week.
Worse still, the ONS reports the number of new homes being built has been slashed again, while rates and inflation still keep rising.
This is not a good recipe, neither for Ibstock (whose shares crashed 10 per cent), nor for growth.
Problems highlighted by our attitude to tax
Oxford-educated Emma Reynolds is the MP who said in a TV interview when asked whether the Budget had broken the tax promises made in Labour’s manifesto: ‘I don’t think employers are working people. They are companies.’
Had Reynolds said this while selling the Morning Star on a street corner, you might laugh out loud. But she is Chief Secretary to the Treasury.
Not only was her tone patronising, but she is utterly wrong and makes a mockery of all those who work day and night running companies.

items.summary: This week, the faces of six independent retailers located in Belfast, Bristol, Manchester, Ilkeston, Gateshead and Glasgow will appear on billboards in their local communities, and on social media, in a campaign created to recognise the contribution of independent local stores in raising more than… This story continues at Independent retailers star in Allwyn ‘Local Retail Champions’ billboard campaign Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
Allwyn UK, operator of The National Lottery, who has funded the campaign, invited these retailers to take part because they have each helped raise more than £1m for Good Causes since they began selling National Lottery tickets and scratchcards in their shops.
The retailers starring in the campaign are:
- Julie Campbell, shopkeeper at Sinclair’s Newsagent in Belfast
- Pinku Patel, store manager of Causeway Card Shop & Newsagents in Bristol
- Aftab Bhatti, Owner of Dynasty News in Glasgow
- Priti Patel, owner of John’s News in Ilkeston
- Umar Nasir, assistant manager of The Paper Shop in Manchester
- Phil Lawrence, co-owner of Choices Newsagent in Gateshead
Alastair Ruxton, chief impact officer at Allwyn UK said: “The £10bn milestone is an incredible achievement by independent retailers, but a number alone doesn’t tell the full story.
“‘Local Retail Champions‘ is about putting the people behind that contribution centre stage and showing the impact independent retailers help make possible in communities across the UK.
“We want independent retailers to feel proud of the role they play in raising much-needed funding for National Lottery Good Causes and for their communities to recognise it too.”
Julie Campbell, shopkeeper at Sinclair’s Newsagent, said: “Our family has been running Sinclair’s Newsagent for 26 years, so it’s lovely to see the shop recognised in this way.
“Raising more than £1.2m for Good Causes across the UK is something we can share with our customers, as they’ve helped make it happen.
“With projects like Templemore Baths here in East Belfast, you can see what National Lottery funding means locally. That makes this feel about much more than having my face on a billboard.”
Pinku Patel, store manager of Causeway Card Shop & Newsagents, said: “To know that National Lottery tickets sold at Causeway Card Shop & Newsagents have helped raise more than £1.5 million for Good Causes across the UK is something we can all be proud of.
“It’s a contribution made possible by our customers, and this campaign is a chance to celebrate that together.
“From local community projects to much-loved Bristol venues, National Lottery funding supports so much across our city. It’s great to know that our shop and customers are playing a part in making that possible.”
The Local Retail Champions campaign launched last month, with films made with three retailers, located in Kent, Wales and West Yorkshire.
They each received a visit from a famous face with a connection to their local area – Joanna Page, presenter and actress, Nicola Adams, the first female boxer to become an Olympic champion Olympian and Matt Weston, double Olympic gold medal skeleton racer at the 2026 Winter Olympic Games.
Allwyn UK has also sent letters to over 22,000 independent retailers who sell National Lottery tickets and scratchcards thanking them for their individual contribution.
Of those, 1,623 shops have raised more than £500,000, 469 have raised more than £1m, and 28 have broken the £2m mark. Remarkably, two shops have each raised more than £3m for Good Causes.
On average, 23p of every pound spent on The National Lottery goes to Good Causes, which has supported more than 680,000 projects across arts, community, heritage and sports since its launch in 1994.

items.body:
London, get ready to meet your new favourite sub.
One of America’s biggest sandwich obsessions, with more than 3,400 restaurants across the US and Canada, is opening its first-ever UK restaurant on Argyll Street on 9th November, bringing its famous freshly made subs to the capital for the very first time.
And to make its London debut one to remember, Jersey Mike’s is treating its first customers to some seriously good perks. The first three people in the queue will win free Jersey Mike’s subs for a year, while the first 50 people through the doors will get a free regular sub.
The countdown is officially on, with the first restaurant opening at 1-4 Argyll Street, just off Oxford Street next week. But this is only the beginning. Jersey Mike’s is bringing its East Coast sandwich game to even more of the capital, with three further London restaurants opening shortly after its debut.
The next openings will see Jersey Mike’s arrive at:
- Baker Street: Mid-November
- New Oxford Street: Late November – close to Tottenham Court Road.
- Cranbourn Street: December 2026 – in the Covent Garden and Leicester Square area.
Founded on the Jersey Shore in New Jersey in 1956, Jersey Mike’s has spent 70 years building a loyal following for its freshly prepared subs. What started as a single neighbourhood sandwich shop has grown into one of America’s best-known sub brands – and now, Londoners can finally find out what the fuss is about.
Forget a grab-and-go sandwich that’s been sitting on the shelf. Jersey Mike’s is all about subs made fresh in-store, with meats and cheeses sliced to order and bread baked throughout the day. From hot, hearty favourites to cold classics, every sub is made to order, with the option to go “Mike’s Way” – topped with onions, lettuce, tomatoes, spices and its signature “The Juice”, an oil blend and red wine vinegar.
The UK launch is being led by Satnam Leihal, CEO of JM Submarines UK Ltd, the master franchisee of Jersey Mike’s in the UK and Ireland.
Peter Cancro, founder of Jersey Mike’s Subs, said: “Bringing Jersey Mike’s to the UK is a special moment for me. From one neighbourhood sandwich shop on the Jersey Shore to more than 3,400 locations across North America, our story has always been about great food, genuine hospitality and the communities we serve.
I’m excited to be working alongside Satnam to bring that same spirit to the UK and Ireland. We share a belief in doing things the right way, building strong teams and creating something that lasts. London is our starting point, and together we see a tremendous opportunity to make Jersey Mike’s a brand people here come to know and love.”
With the first restaurant opening next week and more locations following in quick succession, London’s sub fans won’t have long to wait to get their hands on Jersey Mike’s.

The new flavour pairs a creamy, sweet white chocolate dough with a warm ginger kick, studded with […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! items.body:
Doh!, the ready-to-bake cookie dough brand from BakeAway, is launching its first festive limited edition. White Chocolate & Ginger Cookie Dough lands in Tesco from 9th November with an RSP of £3, available for the Christmas season only.
The new flavour pairs a creamy, sweet white chocolate dough with a warm ginger kick, studded with chunks of white chocolate. It’s built for the moments that fill the weeks before Christmas: friends dropping round, a film night with the kids, something warm after a cold walk home.
Like the core range, it gives shoppers a choice of finish. The on-pack guide sets out 8 minutes for “Gooey Heaven”, 10 minutes for a “Soft Centre” and 13 minutes for “Golden Crunch”, so each household bakes the cookie it likes best. The limited edition arrives in dedicated Christmas packaging with a festive on-pack illustration, giving it clear standout on shelf.
Seasonal innovation for a growing category
Limited editions are a well-worn Christmas tool in biscuits and confectionery. Doh! is bringing that playbook into chilled ready-to-bake dough, a category where the newcomer has already performed well since launch.
Since hitting shelves in April 2026, Doh! has been a standout success for the sweet dough category. In its first 12 weeks, it delivered almost 300% of the category’s net value growth, more than offsetting declines across the rest of the category*. Momentum continued following wider distribution, with Doh! reaching 21% of category value and 18.5% of category units and delivering 112% of category value growth over four weeks*. More recently, it has kept driving incremental growth for the whole category. With Doh!, sweet dough is up 33% in value and 25% in units year on year, and the brand accounts for 81% of category unit growth in the latest 20 weeks**.
Doh!’s own research, commissioned earlier this year with 2,000 UK consumers, found that 79% agree life is too short not to enjoy the occasional sweet treat. Yet more than half (52%) have talked themselves out of one. Christmas is the time of year when that guilt eases, and shoppers spend accordingly. Take-home grocery sales hit a record £13.8 billion in the four weeks to 28 December 2025, up 3.8% year on year***.
A treat that bakes fresh at home in eight minutes fits that festive mood well. For retailers, a time-limited flavour at £3 adds incremental seasonal spend and gives shoppers a reason to buy now rather than later.
Denise Henson, senior brand manager at Doh!, comments: “Christmas is when people stop asking whether they’ve earned a treat and just enjoy one, so it felt like the right moment for our first limited edition. It’s a new reason for Tesco shoppers to head to the chilled aisle at the busiest time of the year, and because it’s only here for Christmas, there’s a real reason to pick it up now.”
Doh! is backed by BakeAway’s largest ever marketing investment in a new brand, with £500,000 committed to supporting the UK launch.
Product at a glance
- Product: Doh! White Chocolate & Ginger Cookie Dough, limited edition
- RSP: £3
- Available: Tesco, from 9th November, for the festive season only
- Where to find it: the chilled aisle, alongside the core Double Choc Chunk and Salted Caramel range

items.title: New stores flatter Primark’s topline, but Europe is the key test ahead of its demerger, says GlobalData

Following today’s release of Primark’s figures for the 12 months ending 12 September 2026; Chloe Tedford-Jones, apparel analyst at GlobalData, a leading intelligence and productivity platform, offers her view: “Primark’s revenue grew 3.5% to £9.8bn in FY2025/26 (ending 12 September 2026), though this was driven entirely by new space, as like-for-like (l-f-l) sales declined 2.6%, […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
Following today’s release of Primark’s figures for the 12 months ending 12 September 2026; Chloe Tedford-Jones, apparel analyst at GlobalData, a leading intelligence and productivity platform, offers her view: “Primark’s revenue grew 3.5% to £9.8bn in FY2025/26 (ending 12 September 2026), though this was driven entirely by new space, as like-for-like (l-f-l) sales declined 2.6%, decelerating further from a 2.3% fall in the previous year. Weak underlying demand reflects a tough value market, as fragile consumer sentiment and squeezed discretionary budgets have led shoppers to cut back on non-essential spend. Adjusted operating profit margin fell 1.7ppts to 10.2%, reflecting heavier discounting pressures following a disappointing festive period earlier in the year and reinvestment in lower prices through its “Iconic Value” initiative. Looking ahead, Primark expects new space to contribute around 4% to sales growth in FY2026/27, with margin held at around 10%, leaving a return to l-f-l growth as the key test ahead of its demerger.
“The UK and Ireland, Primark’s home region, saw total revenue climb 1% and l-f-l’s rise 0.5%, with its UK clothing and footwear market share set to remain stable at 6.1% in 2026. This reflects Primark’s efforts to sharpen price perception, strengthen its product offer, particularly in womenswear, and step up digital marketing. In contrast, Continental Europe remained the key drag, with total sales falling 1% and l-f-l sales down 4.7%, as a stubbornly weak consumer environment and lower brand penetration weighed on sales. Total sales in the US were up 13%, though as Primark states that it remained a difficult region, it can be assumed that growth was purely propped up by new stores, with weak l-f-l‘s.
“Primark’s long-awaited move into home delivery is its most significant operating-model change to date. While timing remains unconfirmed, the shift acknowledges the need to compete with digital-first rivals, and builds on its click and collect growth, with record website sales following the Perrie Sian collaboration. However, fulfilment and returns costs must be tightly managed to preserve its low-price model. The launch is also only confirmed in Great Britain so far, and digital investment remains necessary in Continental Europe to counter online competition and raise brand awareness.
“Store expansion remains the core of Primark’s growth strategy, with the retailer surpassing 500 stores globally following the opening of its Naples store in Italy in September. The US was the primary growth driver, on track for 47 locations by year-end after entering Indiana and Minnesota, as well as a new Manhattan flagship. Middle East expansion is accelerating through its partnership with the Alshaya Group, which added the UAE and Kuwait to Primark’s coverage in FY2025/26, with storss in Bahrain and Qatar opening since the year-end, and a planned Saudi Arabia launch for spring 2027. Meanwhile, a franchise agreement with El Puerto de Liverpool will take Primark into Mexico in the near future, marking its first Latin American entry.”

items.title: Inside ASOS’ AW26 partywear push as ‘going out top’ searches soar 300%
items.summary: The online fashion giant previewed a partywear collection built around bold styling, escapist textures and statement accessories, while offering an early look at the trends set to land in January and February. ASOS has lifted the curtain on its AW26 partywear offer as demand for occasion-led fashion gathers pace, with searches for “going out top”...
items.body:
The online fashion giant previewed a partywear collection built around bold styling, escapist textures and statement accessories, while offering an early look at the trends set to land in January and February.
ASOS has lifted the curtain on its AW26 partywear offer as demand for occasion-led fashion gathers pace, with searches for “going out top” up 300 per cent on its platform.
At a preview held on 03 November, the online retailer showcased a handpicked selection designed to help shoppers build their party-season wardrobes.
The event also gave guests an exclusive first look, and even the opportunity to try on, the trends due to arrive early in 2027.
Pink accents, trending prints and bold animal textures sit at the heart of a party-season collection, which is designed to encourage shoppers to break the rules.
Evening dresses and embellished details add polish, with ASOS positioning the looks as dancefloor-ready options that can carry customers through to morning.
Elsewhere, the retailer is tapping into escapist dressing through a meeting of Western heritage and modern bohemia.
Textured denim, crafted suede, fringing and intricate detailing feature across a palette of sun-baked tans and warm neutrals, giving elevated pieces a well-travelled feel.
Cocktail earrings, textured heels and printed bags provide the collection’s styling punctuation. ASOS is betting on these add-ons as an accessible route to personalisation, allowing shoppers to refresh trusted wardrobe staples and turn them into head-turning outfits.
Looking ahead, romantic dressing takes on a more modern edge.
Fluid draping draws on vintage opulence, while cinched waists temper expressive florals to create a more intentional take on classic femininity.
Decorative prints and rich, nostalgia-inspired textures complete the direction.
The preview was staged at ASOS’ London showroom, which was revamped in July 2024.
The multifunctional space enables the online fashion retailer to create content, hold “intimate activations” and events for ASOS and its brand partners, and host talent.
ASOS will announce its full year results on Thursday 05 November, with its 2026 Christmas campaign to follow later this month.

items.body:
Drinksology Kirker Greer (DKG) has secured a regional listing with Tesco NI for Wilfie Wine, its new dog-themed wine brand developed through its wholly owned PAC Wines business.
Four wines are now available across Tesco stores and online in Northern Ireland.
DKG brings together brand creation, production and distribution across spirits and wine. While its brand-building expertise is best known through spirits, the group also owns PAC Wines, an established wine importer.
Wilfie is the first brand to bring those capabilities together for the retail wine aisle, with Tesco NI providing its first regional retail platform. The range is also available for UK and international distribution across off-trade channels.
The idea behind Wilfie is straightforward: make wine shopping more engaging by combining distinctive, emotion-led design with approachable wines that people will want to buy again.
With shoppers making quick decisions in a busy wine aisle, the range uses illustrations of popular dog breeds to create an immediate visual connection. But the proposition goes beyond the packaging. The entire Wilfie range is vegan and all four wines have been selected for their approachable styles, recognisable grape varieties and distinctive flavour profiles.
Sourced from established wine regions in Italy and France, the range offers a mix of familiar styles and accessible price points. The Veneto Pinot Grigio is crisp and refreshing, with pear and mineral notes, while the Languedoc Sauvignon Blanc delivers grapefruit, passion fruit and subtle herbal flavours. The Languedoc Merlot has ripe cherry and plum character with soft tannins, while the Languedoc Malbec combines mulberry, redcurrant and blueberry with notes of violet, cranberry and cocoa.
Every wine in the range was selected by DKG Wine Director Niall Diver, drawing on the sourcing expertise of PAC Wines.
Michael Crealey, lead packaged buying manager for Tesco NI, said: “We’re delighted to welcome Wilfie Wines to Tesco stores across Northern Ireland. It’s a brilliant example of a local team bringing fresh thinking and real personality to the wine aisle. With its playful dog-led labels and approachable range, Wilfie has plenty of character and really stands out on the shelf. It’s distinctive, memorable and something a little different for our customers, and we’re really pleased to be supporting the team as the brand launches in Tesco.”
The launch comes as dogs play an increasingly important role in UK households. According to UK Pet Food’s 2026 Pet Population Survey, the UK is now home to an estimated 15.5 million dogs, up from 12.5 million in 2021, with 41% of households owning a dog.
The brand takes its name from Wilfie, a cockapoo belonging to DKG’s Ryan McFarland, which also features on the Merlot label alongside a cast of other dogs across the range.
Ryan McFarland, Drinksology Kirker Greer, said: “At DKG, we spend our working lives creating and building spirits brands for ourselves and other brand owners, and we already own a wine business that does brilliantly in the on-trade and specialist stores. Wilfie is what happens when you put those two things in the same room and ask what a retail wine brand should look like.
“The thinking is simple. You have a few seconds to connect with someone at the fixture, so we used beautiful illustrations of popular dog breeds to do that, then made sure the wines delivered the quality and character to match. Niall has done a fantastic job on the liquid and, as always, our creative team have translated that thinking into the design.
“And yes, the brand is named after my cockapoo. The best ideas are sometimes right under your feet!”
The range
Wilfie Pinot Grigio 2025 | Veneto, Italy | 11% ABV | RRP £9.00
An elegant, crisp white with pear and mineral notes, vibrant acidity and a clean, dry finish.
Wilfie Sauvignon Blanc 2025 | Languedoc, France | 11.5% ABV | RRP £11.00
An aromatic white with grapefruit, passion fruit and subtle herbal notes, balanced by bright acidity and a mineral backbone.
Wilfie Merlot 2025 | Languedoc, France | 14% ABV | RRP £11.00
A medium-bodied, velvety red with ripe red cherry and plum flavours, a subtle hint of vanilla, soft tannins and a smooth finish. Wilfie the cockapoo features on the label.
Wilfie Malbec 2025 | Languedoc, France | 13% ABV | RRP £11.00
A smooth, structured red with mulberry, redcurrant and violet notes, alongside crushed blueberry, crème de cassis, cranberry and cocoa.
The range will extend in 2027 with a French rosé and Italian Prosecco, broadening Wilfie’s appeal across key retail wine occasions.
Wilfie Wine is available now in Tesco stores across Northern Ireland, selected independent wine stores, and online at spiritly.com.

items.title: Rackhams launches AI-powered site search with Luigi’s Box ahead of peak trading

items.body:
Rackhams, the online marketplace, has launched a new AI-powered search experience on its website, developed in partnership with search specialist Luigi’s Box. The upgrade goes live ahead of the busiest trading weeks of the year, and is designed to help customers find the products they want more quickly and to surface more of the range from Rackhams’ sellers.
The launch follows a year of exceptional growth. Rackhams’ October sales were more than double those of the same month last year (up 113%), and the product catalogue has grown to more than 350,000 products from over 1,000 sellers. With choice on that scale, helping customers navigate the range matters more than ever.
Smarter, more personal results
The new search uses AI learning, site performance data and personalisation to understand what customers are looking for and show the most relevant results first. A search for “trainers”, for example, can take customers straight to the right category, filtering out products that don’t suit their size or gender so they reach the right options sooner.
The search can also highlight popular products, promote buying guides and show what other customers are searching for. That last feature is useful in gifting periods, giving shoppers a view of what’s popular on site and a source of gift inspiration.
Early results
Since the search was enabled in October, Rackhams has already seen an 8% uplift in daily revenue compared with September, with volume of orders per day up 11%. Rackhams is confident the new search will drive further growth through November and December.
Mike Hart, head of marketing at Rackhams, said: “We’re always striving to make our website a better experience for our customers, and search is at the heart of that. With over 350,000 products on site, we want shoppers to find what they’re looking for quickly and to discover things they didn’t know they needed. A better experience for customers means a more thriving marketplace for our sellers, and that’s what this partnership is about.”
Marianna Szarkova, senior partnerships & expansion manager at Luigi’s Box, said: “We’re really happy to be working with Rackhams. With 350,000 products on the site, it can be hard for shoppers to find what they actually came for, and that’s where our Search & Discovery Suite comes in. It’s great to see the early results already showing a clear daily uplift, and the timing couldn’t be better, with peak season just around the corner.”
